PETITIONS
subsubtopic: FEDERAL BUSINESS DEVELOPMENT BANK-PRIORITY TO SMALL BUSINESSES
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, it is my honour to present a petition pursuant to Standing Order 36. The petitioners state that, in many respects, small businesses in Canada still pay an average tax rate that is higher than Canada's larger businesses. Both the chartered banks and the Federal Business Development Bank give larger firms preferential treatment in financing. The petitioners raise a number of related concerns. The petitioners are asking Parliament to put the Federal Business Development Bank back into the business of making small entrepreneurs its first priority, reducing time-consuming Government red tape for small businesses, and targeting more federal contracts to the small business sector.

subtopic: PETITIONS
subsubtopic: LABELLING OF PRODUCTS TREATED WITH PESTICIDES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have another petition which is also in the appropriate form. The petitioners point out that the human health effects of consuming products treated with pesticides are poorly understood and potentially very harmful.
The petitioners are calling upon Parliament to require all foods treated with pesticides be so labelled, that such labelling include a comprehensive list of all the pesticides used, and that the Government implement a program to encourage and assist farmers to produce a pesticide-free fruit and vegetable sector.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State (Multiculturalism and Citizenship); Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State of Canada
subtopic: PETITIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, pursuant to Standing Order 36, I am very pleased to present a petition to the House of Commons concerning the Rouge River Valley. Some Members have heard of the Rouge River Valley. It is made up of
5,000	precious acres in Scarborough on the boundary of Metro Toronto. It is in the national interest to preserve this wilderness area which contains endangered wildlife species.
The concern of the petitioners, Mr. Speaker, is that the Province of Ontario, which owns this land, is threatening to put a freeway or a garbage dump in the Rouge Valley. On Saturday there was a rally concerning this and I am very pleased to say that the native groups in Ontario have come on board and support the preservation of the Rouge Valley because of the archaeological aspects.
The petitioners join the Mayor of Scarborough, the Minister of the Environment (Mr. Bouchard), the Save the Rouge Valley System group and the Coalition of Scarborough Community Associations in asking Parliament to work with the Government of Ontario to establish the Rouge River Valley as Canadian heritage land or a provincial park.

subtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 81-POST-SECONDARY EDUCATION FUNDING-NATIVE PEOPLES

speechtext:
The House resumed from Friday, April 21, consideration of the motion of Mr. Nault:
That this House recognize that the Government's arbritrary and misanthropic policy of unilaterally capping future funding for postsecondary education for Canada's native peoples severely undermines the right and efforts of these peoples to enhance their capacity to make meaningful and lasting improvements to their economic and social conditions and to establish their self-reliance, thereby condemning them to unacceptable living conditions and driving them to desparate measures; and
That this House urge the Government to terminate its plans to cap this funding and to take steps to establish effective bilateral consultations on this and other matters vital to the improvement of the lives of and the ending of discrimination toward these Native peoples.

subtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 81-POST-SECONDARY EDUCATION FUNDING-NATIVE PEOPLES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to address the issue of post-secondary education funding. First, let me give a bit of background. Changes to the E-12 post-secondary education policy for native students went into effect April 1, 1989. Native people, educators and counsellors across the country have protested against these changes. They feel there is no reason to change a system that has been working sufficiently for First Nations. Protests against these changes have been held across the country since March. There have been letter campaigns, awareness campaigns, a demonstration on Parliament Hill and most recently a national hunger strike. To me, this action is unnecessary. This situation could have been avoided. If the situation is abnormal and out of hand, why did the issue get to a point of people fasting and going on hunger strikes?
The students have asked for three things to make the point very clear that post-secondary education be recognized as a treaty right where there are treaties and an aboriginal right for all native peoples; that a bilateral consultation be established and that a moratorium of one
year be imposed on the implementation of the changes to the policy guidelines.
The Department of Indian and Northern Affairs is proposing policy changes concerning Indian post-secondary education which were to have been implemented April 1, 1989. The post-secondary education budget has been capped without proper consultation with Indian leaders and educators. We recognize that there were 500 consultations. We also recognize that information has not been made available for public consumption.
A priority system for student assistance has been unilaterally developed and a formula funding system for schools has been arbitrarily imposed. This new policy will seriously affect the number of Indian people entering such institutions. This is a key concern. It will also negatively affect students presently enrolled. Students who have been accepted at recognized post-secondary institutions are being denied the opportunity to pursue post-secondary studies because of budgetary restrictions. Travel allowances will not adhere to the student's choice of university or college. This is regressive and restrictive. This is not in keeping with providing a challenge to native peoples to go to where their potential will take them for the very best education they should get. An adherence to a list of approved institutions and disciplines will be required for funding. Cut-backs are designed specifically to reduce the number of Indians entering post-secondary institutions.
There has been much discussion about whether there are cut-backs and how to determine the difference between a cut-back and a capping. With there having been no increase over the last two to three years, that to my mind constitutes a cut-back and is a restriction in the minds of the beneficiaries of the program.
The policy recommendations signify further limits to the possibility of involving more Indian control over education. In the area of consultation there is also a dispute between native people and the Ministry over the quality of consultation that took place prior to the implementation of these changes. Native groups who believe this policy should be a treaty right did not want to jeopardize their position by participating in a consultation with the Ministry, so DIAND received very little feed-back and input to the policy from those people affected. The first five drafts of the policy were done without any consultation with native people. As well, the Minister is not able to document the consultation received or even provide statistics on the alleged problems with the old guidelines which should have justified the need for these changes.
April 24, 1989

This is not a new problem. This is not a problem that the Parties and the leaders have jumped on. It is an old problem. It is something of which the leaders, the Parties and the Members Of Parliament were aware. In a letter to the Right Hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney), Keith Penner, the former critic for aboriginal affairs, said that without consultation with Indian leaders and educators the post-secondary education budget has been capped, that a priority system for student assistance has been unilaterally developed and a formula funding system for schools has been arbitrarily imposed. These measures have resulted in a limitation of access to a program that was previously accessible to all Indian students who qualified for assistance under its provisions. Now Indian students who are eligible for assistance under the program and who have been accepted at recognized post-secondary institutions are being denied the opportunity to pursue post-secondary studies because of budgetary restrictions.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I was about to refer to a quotation on the issue of post-secondary education. Its importance can be expressed by the native population across Canada far more eloquently than by myself, so I will rely on a lot of material I have accumulated from those particular groups during my research.
The first is a quotation from the priorities outlined by the Saskatchewan Indian Education Council of the Federation of Saskatchewan Indians, which was addressed to the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development (Mr. Cadieux). This group has an outline within the presentation entitled "Misplaced Priorities". They state:
Another thing wrong with the policy and attitude of government is that its priorities are misplaced. The Government says these are tough times, and everyone has to tighten their belt. We agree-because if Canada wanted to spend wisely and prudently, the First Nations would be a lot better off than they are now.
Look at the way priorities are set now:

April 24, 1989
Supply
When it comes to paying the costs of holding our youth in jail there seems to be no shortage of money.
When it comes to paying for a lifetime of welfare and poverty, the money is there.
The first priority should be money for our youth who want to move ahead to get an education.
Surely a government should understand investment, even if it doesn't seem to understand human suffering and wasted lives. It should know that a bit of money invested today in education will save a lot on social assistance funds in the future.
This brings to mind the remarks of another senior elder of the population. He said: "If it costs $30,000 for a majority of the native students who are educated and get post-secondary education, that is paid back through the tax system in spades". It is not as if they are ripping off the taxpayers.
The Saskatchewan Indian Education Council went on to say:
What does it cost for education for a young man or a young woman to be self-supporting? $30,000? What does it cost for that same young man or woman to be supported for the rest of his years on welfare, or to be counted as a casualty of one of the unemployed-$50,000-a half-a-million dollars?
These are questions people ask.
And that doesn't count for the cost of foster care and social disorganization -not to mention the cost of losing the contribution to society of a productive, capable human being. It is incredible that Canada would be willing to support a young person on welfare, but prohibit the same money being used to support that your person's education.
If there ever was a shortsighted policy that would be paid over and over for generations ahead, it is one the Department has invented for post-secondary education.
We would think, too, that a Canadian Government and the people of Canada would want to see that its money was well-spent. It hasn't been well spent under the past policy, and it won't be well-spent under the new policy.
The policies force us to waste money. The most effective solutions cannot be applied because they are 'against policy'. Students are forced to take inappropriate decisions in order to conform with an inflexible policy.
What seems to be the most important priority for the Department is maintaining control, maintaining poverty, maintaining Indians in their place. There is no better evidence to this harsh statement than the policy which the Department is trying to force on the First Nations.
Let's sit down together and decide where the priorities lie, and how we can most efficiently and effectively conserve valuable resources.
These statements can easily be misconstrued or misinterpreted. But if you take the time to listen, what people want is to play a meaningful role in a bilateral process that is being discussed. They want to have input into a policy that is workable for them. They are the ones who
have to deal with this particular policy. They are the ones who are going to the post-secondary institutions under this policy. They want their leaders and their students to participate in a meaningful dialogue in order to come up with a meaningful policy that they can live with and work with.
I want to remind the House of the statement made by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) at the First Ministers Conference in April, 1985. He said:
As a Canadian and as the Prime Minister, I fully recognize and agree with the emphasis that the aboriginal peoples place on having their special rights inserted into the highest law of the land, protected from arbitrary legislative action. Constitutional protection for the principle of self-government is an overriding objective because it is the constitutional manifestation of a relationship, an unbreakable social contact between aboriginal peoples and their governments.
In seeking constitutional change, I recognize that this alone cannot resolve our economic problems. Constitutional change is not enough to reduce disparities and correct injustices. Rather, improvements to the economic and social circumstances of aboriginal peoples must be pursued at the same time as changes to our Constitution are sought to define the rights of aboriginal peoples. Action is required on both fronts and the two set of endeavours, while separate, are mutually supportive.
Why do we have the statement in 1985, and why do we have a Minister whose actions are contrary to the statement of support for the aboriginal peoples in adherence to the contract between the aboriginal peoples and the Government?
I want to bring forward another article that came out of a book from a group of 38 elders who were asked to repeat their life history. Many of these elders received their education on the land. Many went to residential schools and many did not have the benefit of a full education, going only to Grade 8. For example, Willy Minoza who was born in 1924. "In 1936, my father died and my mother was not able to look after me. So I went to the mission." Willy feels that the mission failed to give him the educational background that would have enabled him to succeed in the white man's world. He says, "Our lives run parallel with the white man's, parallel and never touching. It is unlikely that we will ever be able to do and have what white people have, and for me there is no use in trying to change things. I may as well live out my days in my own way rather than to struggle to no purpose." He goes on to say, "When they tell us the land is ours, I don't believe what they say. If it was ours, then we would have control, and we don't. If we had self-determination, then we would have a chance."
April 24, 1989

As a young aboriginal person I have dealt with many of the students across Canada. I have taught elementary school, high school, junior high school, in the colleges and the university. I feel that we deal with the same kind of hopelessness. We have to compel the young native people to overcome the kind of attitude that is being perpetuated by a lack of trust between the Government and the native people. I think the one key to self-determination and self-sufficiency is through education.
To put a cap on the education program is a move that is regressive, that holds back native people. You may sit back and say that we have a Cadillac approach to education. I do not believe that. Many of the native students come from large families where wealth is shared with everyone. I know that for a fact. I come from a family of 18. I feel that the native population rallies around this issue and they support one another. We cannot afford to have a priority or a waiting list. We need every native individual that is qualified and able to get a post-secondary education enabled to do that. We do not need impediments. We do not need a Government that will not work with the people. We need a Government on side that recognizes its mandate to work with the aboriginal peoples of Canada.
We should not lay blame and control the dialogue and have the native people pitted against the non-native population on this issue.
An example of native people getting support from students and from other groups across Canada is a statement from Milasapina College in B.C. It says, "Milasapina College strongly supports the Nanaimo Indians band's protest of proposed First Nations post-secondary funding capping by Indian and Northern Affairs for the following reasons: One, post-secondary education is one of the most important tools in providing the profile of native people in society. Native bands have indicated for many years that post-secondary education is their number one priority. Three, caping the funds needed for post-secondary education is certainly going to limit who gets educated, and will possibly direct people into select programs. Four, all Canadian peoples have a right to an education, and because of their unique constitutional status, the aboriginal people have a very special right to that education. Five, at Milasapina College, the number of native students have increased from 11 students in 1974 to 150 in 1989 on all four campuses."
Supply
It is interesting to note that over the years, there has been waste. There have been periods of times in which the program funding has not been maximized or used efficiently, but it is now at this critical time that people of my generation and the younger people that I see coming up are starting to reap the benefits of that program. They are starting to re-invest into society in a positive way. This particular cap is an impediment to that positive movement.
I want to read a letter from John D. Whyte, the dean of the Faculty of Law of Queen's University. It is entitled:"Statement of support in the face of government cut-backs in native Canadian post-secondary student assistance program". He states:
Any adjustments to the government program of funding higher education for native students which limits access to university training constitutes a devastating blow to the program of producing social justice for native people.
According to the Human Rights Commissioner's Report, this is the essence of where the Government has to go with aboriginal peoples. Your efforts have to be directed at helping, not impeding. That is what the people are asking for. We are not asking for something that we are not entitled to.
I would also like to read another letter that comes from Joanne Martin, National Affairs for the Canadian Union of Educational Workers. She sends greetings of solidarity to the Assembly of First Nations. She states:
"We support your demand that the federal Government rescind the changes made to the Post-Secondary Education Assistance Program and your call for a moratorium on changes to the old policy. We call on the Government to commence negotiations with the Assembly of First Nations immediately. In solidarity and friendship, Joanne Martin."
I have files full of these letters from people across Canada who believe that this change is going to affect the way in which native people can participate equitably in society. I have met with the students on the fast. I have personally, for health reasons, asked those students to come off the fast. I have also done that because I believe this is not a problem that resulted from the fast. This issue was there before, something that the leadership recognized. When I first got here in December, my first delegation was from Saskatchewan. They immediately provided me with documents on this issue expressing their concern. I then had my staff meet with a group of university students. I have met with people all across Canada from B.C. to Newfoundland on this particular issue. They all expressed their particular concern.

April 24, 1989
Supply
In closing, I would like to say on the issue of treaty rights that many people will say it is not a treaty right. The Minister has agreed to provide a forum for discussion, once the situation normalizes itself. Well, I am not sure that this opportunity will come this week. We will soon be consumed with budgetary discussion. The importance of this item will be diminished by all of the activities evolving around Budget, but I can tell you that it will not diminish in the hearts of the people it affects. It will not diminish in importance with the leaders. It is something that the leaders believe in and will struggle to obtain equality in. I want to thank you very much.

speechtext: Madam Speaker, I do not have a copy of the list of students who will not be able to attend post-secondary education, but I believe that there have been three regional reports showing that in one area, there is a waiting list of 500 native students who qualify but who will not be able to attend post-secondary education facilities because of the capping.

subtopic: SITTING RESUMED The House resumed at 11.41 a.m.
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I too want to pass along congratulations for the Hon. Member's well-argued reaction to the Government's behavior surrounding the question of capping post-secondary education funds for native students. The last question asked of the Hon. Member dealt with the number of people who will be unable to pursue post-secondary educational goals.
April 24, 1989

One of the bands in my constituency, the Neskainlith Indian Band, has been a very progressive band in the last number of years. It is a small band and it has a list of 30 young people who have now qualified for entrance to post-secondary institutions. The band has been informed by the Department of Indian Affairs that it will be lucky to receive funding to send five students. This means that 25 young people from that small band in rural western Canada who have worked to qualify for post-secondary education will not be able to have that opportunity.
In the best interests of the pursuit of native self-government, self-reliance and self-determination, education at the post-secondary level is absolutely mandatory. My colleagues and I in the New Democratic Party find it unacceptable that these opportunities would not be provided for native young people.

subtopic: SITTING RESUMED The House resumed at 11.41 a.m.
speechtext: Madam Speaker, all I can say is that I agree that the situation is unacceptable.

speechtext: Madam Speaker, the Hon. Member stated that funding for the program has not increased over the past two years. The program budget has increased by 10 per cent per year for the last two years. How can the Hon. Member make such a misleading statement?

speechtext: Madam Speaker, I think that the misleading information is coming from the Government. I did mention the 10 per cent increase in my remarks, but I also mentioned that the budget remains at $130 million. A 10 per cent increase over the next three years could be far more easily negotiated between the various groups on a per annum basis and would be preferable to a 10 per cent that remains static over the three years. I do not see that as being a major increase or as keeping up with the times and with the challenging demands of getting a state-of-the- art education in 1989.

Madam Speaker, the issue is not about students on an individual basis. If we looked at every case in any crisis situation, I am sure we could find positive elements.
The issue is that we do not want a waiting list to be created by the capping. That is the issue.

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I would first like to congratulate the Hon. Member for Western Arctic (Ms. Blondin) on her comments and on the obvious feeling she has imparted to them. My constituency of Kootenay-West Revelstoke is perhaps one of the few hinterland or resource ridings in Canada that has no Indian bands or reserves within its boundaries. However, I have worked for a number of years at different times in the past with a number of band councils, particularly in British Columbia and Manitoba, and I am aware of some of the history of the issue.
The problem that I see and I think many of us see is that the Government continues to deal with this in a narrow, legalistic way, saying it is not capped in a narrow definition of the term. Government Members continually ask, as they asked of the Hon. Member, whether or not her Party or our Party or any Hon. Member believes that these potential student rights are a treaty right.
For decades in the past, in coastal areas of British Columbia, our white, Christian churches imparted the belief to many native students that there was nothing in their background to be proud of, and that they should be ashamed of their families and their history. Now we have finally reached the point where they are proud of themselves and proud and aware of their history, in the same manner that the rest of us have had that luxury for years and years. They are now claiming what is a moral imperative and a right which must be recognized, not in

April 24, 1989
Supply
its narrow legalistic terms, but by realizing if they are now prepared and want to exercise their abilities to the fullest of their potential that nothing should stand in the way. I believe that that is the argument we are all making. We have heard enough of the narrow, legalistic defences brought forward by the Government.

speakeroldname: Hon. Kim Campbell (Minister of State (Indian Affairs and Northern Development)):
speakerposition: Minister of State (Indian Affairs and Northern Development)
subtopic: SITTING RESUMED The House resumed at 11.41 a.m.
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, before I begin I want to make a brief comment on two things stated. The previous speaker suggested that the issue of treaty right is a narrow, legalistic approach. I wish to advise the Hon. Member that the question of whether or not post-secondary education is or is not a treaty right is the fundamental basis for the current dispute between the Government and Indian people over this policy.
As a matter of policy, the Government has shown a deep commitment to post-secondary education for native students, and the question of whether or not it is a treaty right underlines most of the argument we are hearing now. The Hon. Member, like myself, is from British Columbia which is not a treaty province, but I can assure the Hon. Member that if he had accompanied me to Saskatchewan yesterday he would not have made the remarks that he did.
The Hon. Member for Western Arctic (Ms. Blondin) objects very strongly to the problem that we do not have a data base. Yet she denounces the very guidelines that, for the first time, will enable us to establish the data base of aboriginal students in Canada. This will enable the Government to plan both fiscally and educationally. I find that rather an extraordinary position for the Hon. Member to take.
I would also like to remind the Hon. Member that, in response to a question from the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development (Mrs. Dobbie), the Hon. Member for Notre-Dame-de-Grace (Mr. Allmand), a former Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development, stated in debate on Friday: "At no time did I say the Government has cut back on the program. They have not. They have increased the program". It would sometimes be a welcome development in the House for members of the Opposition to have the good grace to recognize that.
The Opposition paints a very gloomy picture of the conditions of native people in Canada and, yes, it has been well documented that Indian living conditions, for example, lag behind those of the general Canadian population in many ways. What I find disappointing about the Opposition's view of Indian conditions is its lack of balance and perspective. There appears to be a belief that aboriginal people are totally dependent on the federal Government. The Government is supposed to provide shelter, the Government is supposed to provide employment, the Government is to develop the human resources of native communities, and the Government is even to provide self-government.
Anyone who knows the native people of Canada knows that they are not sitting back waiting for Government to save them. More and more Indians and Inuit are taking their futures into their own hands. Indian political leaders and ordinary community members are the people who are building self-government. The right to self-government is part of every Canadian's birthright, and aboriginal Canadians are no exception.
Indian entrepreneurs are building businesses and creating employment across the country, from Sumas Clay Products near Vancouver to Econobois in Huron Village, Quebec; from Six Nations in Ontario to Eskaso-ni on Cape Breton Island, the elders are forming the young in the ways of their native cultures, as the schools are preparing them for a modern technological society.
Health is more than pills and hospitals; it is sound lifestyles. It is communities such as Alkali Lake in my own Province of British Columbia renouncing alcoholism through the courage of their own members.
So let us not insult aboriginal Canadians by portraying them as passive wards of the state. That era of total dependence is thankfully passing into history. Nevertheless, the fact remains that Government has an important supporting role to play in native development.
Social indicators show that Indians generally face worse living conditions than other Canadians. For example, life expectancy for Indians is about eight years shorter than the Canadian average. Death by suicide is about two and a half times more common among Indians than among the general Canadian population. Death from injury and poisoning is four times more common. The unemployment rate of on-reserve Indians is several times the Canadian average. These facts are undeniable. They represent unfinished business for Canadian society, and we acknowledge that.
April 24, 1989

Yet why must there always be this litany of negativism? Rather, we should take heart in the stunning progress which has occurred over the past generation, and especially in the past 10 years. We need historical perspective in order to understand and deal with the remaining problems.
Since 1960 Canadian society has opened up to Indian people politically, economically, and socially. Indians themselves have acted with initiative and determination. Moreover, federal government programs and budgets benefiting Indians have expanded rapidly. The result has been a generation of remarkable advance.
Until 1961 Indians did not have the right to vote in federal elections. Today Indians participate in Canadian political life at all levels. Indians have served and continue to serve as government Ministers and elected and appointed representatives. In the four constitutional conferences on aboriginal self-government native leaders negotiated directly with the Prime Minister and the provincial premiers.
In 1960 most Indian communities were still directed by Indian agents, officials appointed by the federal Government. Today the Indian agents have long disappeared, and Indians directly administer over two-thirds of the funding provided by the Indian and Inuit affairs program of the Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development.
Some bands, such as the Cree and Naskapi in northern Quebec, and the Sechelt in British Columbia have established their own self-government structures outside the Indian Act, and several more communities are developing their own arrangements in consultation with the federal Government.
In the area of education we have seen that in the 1960s Indians had little role in their own education. Many students were sent to church-run residential schools where their language and culture were discouraged, and where they were cut off from their families and their communities. Few Indians graduated from high school, and virtually none went on to post-secondary education.
Today there are approximately 250 band-managed schools, up from 135 in 1980-81, serving over 26 per cent of Indian students. Indian language, culture, and tradition are increasingly being integrated into the curriculum, often employing Indian elders as instructors. The
Supply
proportion of Indians on the staff of federal schools has tripled during the last two decades.
There is significant evidence of improved educational performance. For example, in 1984 the Canadian Education Association reported: "a sharp improvement in academic achievement" of Indian students.
Improvement in post-secondary education over the years has also been dramatic. In the 1960s not more than a few hundred Indian students were enrolled in post-secondary studies. In 1975-76, 2,071 Indian students were assisted with a budget of more than $4 million. On a personal note, I might add that as a professor of Political Science in the University of British Columbia in that year, I had the pleasure of teaching one of those students who went on to successfully complete the program in native law at the University of British Columbia. Since then the number of students assisted has grown to the point where last year over 15,000 students were funded from a budget of $130 million.
The new program provides a range of monthly grants for living expenses ranging from $290 per month for a single student to $1,405 for a single parent with four dependants. In addition, the program covers the cost of tuition, travel, books and other special equipment required for the course. No other country offers its native students such a generous program.
The policy was changed to improve the effectiveness of the program and to encourage more Indian and Inuit graduates to pursue careers that would contribute to the achievement of Indian self-government and economic independence, reflecting two important goals of native people. The new program rules support those goals more effectively than the old. The new policy does not cut back on funding. There is no cap on the budget of the Post-secondary Student Assistance Program. As other colleagues have stated, the budget has increased by 10 per cent in each of the last two years to keep up with the growing demand for funding.
If the data indicate that more increases are required in the future, my colleague, the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development (Mr. Cadieux) has stated on numerous occasions that he is prepared to seek increased financial resources. The old policy limited the length of student support to a specific number of student months. Under the new policy there will be no 48-month

April 24, 1989
Supply
limit on assistance about which we keep hearing. That was only a proposal for discussion which was changed after last year's consultation with approximately 500 bands, tribal councils and student groups.
Taking into consideration the views of these groups, the new policy provides funding for the time it normally takes to obtain degrees right up to the doctorate level. Additionally, the policy will provide funding for an extra year, if necessary, in order that students can complete each of those degrees.
Previously there was a wide range of regionally determined rates of assistance. The new policy establishes a national standard rate structure providing more equal treatment across Canada. The new policy improves an already successful program and reflects many concerns expressed by native groups before and during the consultation held last year. It increases funding assistance, and promotes self-government and economic self-reliance through strategic study scholarships of up to $3,500 per year. It promotes excellence through academic scholarships of up to $1,000 per year.
I want to add my opinion to that of my colleagues that I believe this new policy is fair and a great improvement over the previous guideline. Education is definitely seeing some progress.
Concerning the area of housing, in the 1960s most Indians lived in seriously inadequate housing. In 1965, for example, fewer than half of on-reserve houses had electricity and only one in six had a safe water supply. Piped water and sewage systems were virtually non-existent. New houses being built did not meet basic national building standards, let alone satisfy the special needs resulting from the traditional life style and harsh climate of many communities. Crowding was a serious problem. Today, two-thirds of Indian homes have sewers or septic tanks, electricity is available in virtually all communities. With the assistance of federal funds of $118 million allocated for on-reserve housing together with loans guaranteed by the federal Government Indian bands build about 3,000 new homes and renovate another 3,500 each year. This total consistently exceeds the minimum targets that have been established.
More than 30 per cent of the current housing stock has been built in the last five years alone and a further 35 per cent has been renovated. Housing is being built to national building code standards using Indian labour and materials where possible and is being designed to meet cultural and climatic conditions. The health of Canadian Indians has improved considerably over recent years. These changes are the result of improved living conditions, better access to quality health care and greater community involvement in health education and delivery. Life expectancy is a significant indicator of over-all quality of life in a given population.
Between 1978 and 1985 life expectancy at birth for Indian males increased from 61.6 years to 64 years and for Indian women from 68.9 to 72.8 years. The rate of increase for both sexes is about double that for the general Canadian population. Although life expectancy for both sexes still lags about eight years behind the over-all population, the gap is narrowing.
Twenty years ago few Indian businesses existed except for family farm operations and some local stores. Most reserves imported goods and services. Employment was generally limited to traditional activities such as trapping, fishing and hunting. Indians had little control or involvement in planning or managing their own economic development programs. Isolation from urban centres, relatively low levels of education, especially among older workers, lack of business experience and capital and legal obstacles all imposed barriers to on-reserve economic development. However, progress is being made. Today, there are over 5,000 Indian businesses most of which are located on reserves and are individually owned. About half of these businesses have been established in the last five years. The Government has been instrumental in helping them get started with money and advice but the vast majority are now self-sustaining.
In 1986-87 alone the Indian and Northern Affairs Economic Development Program helped over 900 Indian businesses through a combination of equity contributions, direct loans and loan guarantees. Indians are now able to meet many of their local reserve needs for transportation, construction and the supply and distribution of basic commodities. Reserve-based enterprises are active in the mainstream of Canada's strong resource sector with significant involvement in the oil, gas, minerals, forestry, including sawmills, and agricultural sectors.
April 24, 1989

The economy of Indian communities has benefited significantly from the devolution of government-funded Indian programs such as band administration, social welfare, education and economic development to the community level. To date, this political development has led to more than 8,500 jobs being created by band governments.
Over the last decade there has been a major increase in the involvement of Indians in the planning, management and provision of economic development programs. To date, the federal Government has aided Indians in assuming control of such programs by providing assistance to Indian financial and sectoral economic development institutions, tribal level development corporations and band economic development officers.
In the early 1960s, Indian culture was only beginning to emerge from a long period of neglect. Indian language and religion had increasingly fallen into disuse. The younger generation was mostly ignorant of the traditional practices and pursuits that had for centuries sustained Indian communities.
Today, Indian culture is being reasserted as a key to community pride and self-reliance. Native language programs have been instituted in the schools along with programs on Indian culture and history. About 50 per cent of Indian students now receive instruction in their native languages. There are numerous aboriginal newspapers, several of which are multilingual, publishing in a native language as well as either English or French. An extensive network of aboriginal radio and TV services provide native language programming to aboriginal communities. The work of Indian artists is increasingly being accepted by the mainstream art community. Works by native artists hang in galleries across Canada, including the National Gallery in Ottawa.
Indian communities are gaining control of their future. Individual Indians have choices never before available to them. They can choose to live on reserve close to their traditional lands and pursuits or they can choose to live in the cities and participate in a broader society. Moreover, they can choose a lifestyle which draws upon what both worlds have to offer.
The important advances made by Canada's Indian people can be attributed to several factors, one of the most important is the determination and preservation of a new generation of Indian leaders and professionals. In Government today there are not unlimited funds nor is
Supply
progress as quick as many demand. The fact is, however, that federal expenditures for aboriginal affairs have increased significantly in recent years. In 1984-85, total federal expenditures for aboriginal peoples were $2.7 billion. By 1988-89, these expenditures reached $3.4 billion. As a percentage of total federal expenditures, excluding public debt costs, expenditures for aboriginal affairs increased from 3.13 per cent in 1984-85 to 3.42 per cent in 1988-89. This represents a very significant re-direction of Government resources, especially during a time of expenditure restraint.
Indian living conditions have improved significantly in the last quarter century. Although much has been accomplished, of course, more remains to be done. Indians are still among the most disadvantaged of all Canadians. Nevertheless, the momentum for change, established over the last 25 years, is clear and strong. The federal Government is firmly committed to working with Indian communities to achieve further improvement in the years ahead. Such improvements will come with the direct involvement of educated professionals, hence the importance of the post-secondary student assistance program. This policy equips the Indian youth of today with the knowledge and skills necessary to enhance self-government and economic self-sufficiency tomorrow.

The Hon. Minister denied that there was a cap being placed on the budget for the post-secondary education program. The Member will also recognize that the participation rate for native students is 4 per cent, while the participation rate for the population as a whole is something in the neighbourhood of 27 per cent. It is obvious that there is a racial bias against the participation of native Indians.
The time to place a cap on the budget for post-secondary education is not when there is such a substantial degree of inequity between the participation rate of natives and the participation rate in the population as a whole.
The Minister has said in her speech, before she went on to other issues, that there was no capping of the budget. I wonder if she could explain the following statement made in the Minister's letter of March 20: "A budget that could not continue to grow at the pace of the last decade", in other words, using everything but the words,"the budget is being capped." The growth is being curtailed in that budget.
In many other places in the same letter, Madam Speaker, the Minister is making the same statement about the budget being curtailed, such as that we "will have to live within its annual allocation, which may mean that a small number of students will temporarily have to seek those sources of support available to all other Canadians".
The participation rate figures suggest that Indians are being denied access to those sources of support available to all other Canadians. Will the Minister admit that the budget is being capped, in the former Minister's own words, although he does not use the word "capped", and that he is doing it at a time when there is a significant inequity between the participation rate of native students and the participation rate in post-secondary education of Canadians as a whole?

speakerposition: Minister of State (Indian Affairs and Northern Development)
subtopic: SITTING RESUMED The House resumed at 11.41 a.m.
speechtext:
I welcome the opportunity to address the Hon. Member's comments because the Leader of his Party raised the issue of the Minister's letter on Friday during this debate. Unfortunately, there was not enough time to pursue his remarks.
The Minister comments in his letter that the budget cannot continue to expand at the rate of the last decade. In the last decade, or if I can just expand, since the program began, which is really 14 years, the budget increased by a factor of 30, when the student enrolment increased by a factor of 7.5. That is an enormous increase. It is now timely, I believe, and that is the view of the Government. It is time to look at the program and to see whether it is getting the results and whether it is as effectively managed as it could be. The purpose of the new guidelines is to try to ensure that. We have, for example, no firm data that enables us to plan carefully in advance for the demands on the post-secondary program.
We believe, from what we have been able to ascertain, that the demographics of the student population is shifting slightly. The enormous initial demand from mature students is levelling off. Those are the students that tend to have dependants, and require a greater level of support. The balance of the age groups and students will change slightly, that we will see more young, single students coming into the stream. They do not get support at the same level because they do not have dependants, and they do not require child care and increased levels of support for housing.
We are trying to get hold of the program to understand who our clientele is and what the future demands are going to be. That is the purpose of the program. I do not think that to suggest that the program budget cannot increase 30 times in the next decade is in some way an implication that we do not want to support native students. We have many programs in this Government to which we allocate budgetary funding. We want to do it on the most accurate basis. The problem that we have had in the past is that sometimes we have had indications of
April 24, 1989

funding needs in one part of the country, and those funds have not been used, and in other parts of the country students have been kept waiting.
We have made the commitment that there will be no denials of funding. There may be deferrals for a term. We are hoping that there will not be deferrals. We are hoping that in fact we can have a system where our information is sufficiently complete so that all of the students will be able to study as soon as they are ready to do so.
I would think that there would be an attempt to try to understand a very important part of the budget, to get some control of it, to find out what the demand is, so that the Minister can always be well supported when he goes to Treasury Board. In an era of difficult fiscal restraint, we are looking at an enormous national debt, when all of the Departments of the Government have an obligation to the Canadian people to manage well. I find it extraordinary that the Eton. Member would be opposed to provisions which will enable the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development always to present a well substantiated request to Treasury Board, a well substantiated proposal for funding of this program. The commitment of the Government to this program is not simply theoretical or rhetorical. It is palpable. It has grown by 34 per cent since we came into Government. That is the proof of the pudding.
I think it is extremely important to understand that there are other issues surrounding this particular debate. Certainly, the question of treating the post-secondary assistance program as a budgetary matter, as opposed to something that is open-ended and funded with a blank cheque, is a reflection of the position that the treaty Indians take, that post-secondary education is a treaty right. There is a philosophical issue underlying this. It is a serious one. It is one that will not be resolved in the near future.
I think that to suggest that the Minister's letter suggesting a concern that a program cannot expand by a factor of 30 in the next decade, is in some way a reflection of a hostility to the program, or a desire to cut it back, is ridiculous. Clearly, what we want is a program that meets the needs and that our Department can fund with some knowledge and some assurance, and where
Supply
our requests for funding will be met with approval and respect by Treasury Board.

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, it is a pleasure for me to have this opportunity to speak in this debate and to discuss this extremely important issue. Over the weekend I took the opportunity to read through some of the statements that have been made by the Minister and by other participants in this debate. I noticed that the Minister's speech in the House was designed to reassure us and to try to cool out the issue.
In opening his remarks, he said he believed that we were closer together on this issue than the controversy would seem to suggest. Then he did what the Minister of State for Indian Affairs (Ms. Campbell) did, which was to read through a series of programs and post-secondary education guidelines. He then came to a point in his speech at which he said he did not believe that post-secondary education is a treaty right. When everyone who was listening to the debate felt that perhaps we were getting closer together, we ended up poles apart.

April 24, 1989
Supply
In his letter of March 20, 1989, the Minister clearly stated that he believes that references to education and to schools in the treaties could not refer to post-secondary education. Ele was making an absolutely unilateral interpretation of a treaty. As the Minister of State just suggested, that is where one of the problems lies in the debate concerning this issue. It is what relationship post-secondary education has to treaty rights and aboriginal rights. It is an issue which needs to be clearly negotiated and discussed between the natives involved and the Ministry.
As far as the Indians are concerned, the suggestion that post-secondary education is not a treaty right or an aboriginal right is dead wrong. Indians perceive post-secondary education funding to be a part of the obligation that has been established between Canada and the original owners of the country. They are as convinced of that as they are convinced of anything. For the Minister to state as he did in his letter, and as he repeated again in his speech on Friday, that he does not believe that the references in the treaties refer to post-secondary education is a beads and blankets approach to the interpretation of those treaties.
It is unfitting of a Minister in this day and age. It does not recognize the more modern treaties that have sought post-secondary education on the part of the participants in those treaties and agreements. The Minister seems to have gone back to the 1900s in order to get his interpretation of what the natives and the signatories to those treaties actually meant when they agreed to schools on reserves and to education provisions.
The Minister's statement ignores the spirit and the intent of the treaties which was to provide Indians of the day and, supposedly, future generations of Indians the same quality, the same type and the same access to education that was available to non-Indians throughout Canada. The Minister is attempting to freeze those treaties in time. Unfortunately, that creates a problem in the debate around native post-secondary education.
Around the time of the 1890s Ministers did not seem to have very much compunction about unilateral interpretation of provisions of treaties. Where treaties provided for education or schools on reserves, the Ministers of Indian Affairs during that time, as well as the Superintendents General of Indian Affairs, decided that they could re-jig that requirement in a treaty and provide for residential schools, in some cases hundreds
of miles away from the reserves where the treaties required them to locate residential schools.
We all know from the reports of Superintendents General of Indian Affairs exactly what was the purpose of residential schools. The parliamentarians, the politicians and the administrators in the Department of Indian Affairs of the day felt that until they could remove Indian children from their culture, their family life, their communities and their language and deprive them of those three things, they would not be able to convert those Indian children into non-Indian children. That was the fundamental reason behind the residential school system. It was to take kids away from their parents and to destroy their family life and all of the cultural reinforcers that they had in their own communities in their own language on the reserve. It was to destroy their culture and try to mass produce them as white Indians.
The program was an abysmal failure. Fortunately, it was an abysmal failure from the point of view of those who wanted to foist the programs on the natives. It did not work in spite of the attempt to destroy culture among native students because the reinforcers were there. The parents constantly came back into the lives of their children. The language persisted. The concept of community, self-government, nationhood and ownership of land persisted, in spite of legislation passed in this assembly over the years to try to deprive Indians of those rights.
In spite of the residential school system, the culture of native groups persisted. That is a veiy positive failure, if I can put those two words together. The failure of the residential school system has allowed Indians of the day an idea of what their culture, self-government and languages are.
The residential school system was a unilateral interpretation by the federal Government and authorities of the Department of Indian Affairs as to how they could meet their obligations under the treaties that they had signed with Indians and Indian nations. When natives look to the recent unilateral interpretation by the Minister of Indian Affairs when he said that those references and treaties do not apply to post-secondary education, it is no wonder they suspect the motives of the Minister as being precisely the same as the Minister of Indian Affairs who set up the residential school system in opposition to the treaty provisions many, many years ago. They have a legitimate right to be suspicious of the Minister in his unilateral interpretation that those references in treaties do not apply to post-secondary education.
April 24, 1989

As the signatories of the day understood the treaties, they were to be living documents. They were not designed to freeze native Indians in time. They were not beads and blankets documents. They were designed as the basis of a continuing, growing and evolving relationship between Indian nations and the Canadian nation. They were designed as living documents to reflect the circumstances of the day. If it was appropriate in 1850, 1860 and 1870 to provide elementary or secondary education or schools on the reserves, then it is appropriate in interpreting those treaties today to understand them in a different set of circumstances. It is legitimate for natives in treaty areas to consider those references in treaties related to education and schools to refer just as accurately to post-secondary education as they referred to elementary and secondary education in previous times.
For the Minister to attempt to freeze those treaties back in the 1900s is unfitting of him. It is unfitting of the Government. There absolutely needs to be a process of interpreting treaties, especially as to what they mean in the current time today. There has to be some new type of agreement signed between the treaty nations and the Government to determine a process by which treaties are reviewed, by which they are brought up to date and by which their spirit and intentions are agreed upon in modern circumstances. Those things absolutely need to be done. What the Minister has done in his letter of March 20 is interpret and state his belief that the provisions in the treaty do not provide post-secondary education. He has done it unilaterally. He has no right to do it as a right of his office. He can only do it through a formal structure established between himself as a representative of this Government and the Indian nations.
When the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Indian Affairs (Mrs. Dobbie) asks us if our Party believes that post-secondary education is a treaty right, it is not our Party which can state that. It is to be decided through a process of interpretation by the signatories of those treaties. It is an obligation. There has to be a forum established to do that in which the people who signed the treaties are represented equally, and where the decision gives equal representation to both sides involved in the signing of that treaty.
Supply
That issue has to be resolved. One of the major difficulties that the Minister has thrown in the path of resolving this problem, one of the major roadblocks created, is his firm and adamant statement that he does not believe that those treaty provisions relate to post-secondary education. He has created a problem that is going to be very difficult to negotiate.
I understand that some of the prairie treaty people and the Federation of Saskatchewan Indians are developing documents which will set up a process for interpreting treaties so that we can use them as living documents and make them apply to today's circumstances. Any reasonable person sitting down to interpret these treaties would agree that, while they may have referred to elementary or secondary education in the 1850s, they would certainly refer to higher levels of education now. Before the Minister makes any change in the post-secondary education financing programs of this Government, he has an obligation to put in place a method, a process, a forum for discussing how these treaties are to be interpreted. It is a key issue in this debate. It is an issue that treaty natives and natives across this country fear. If the Minister is allowed to interpret these issues unilaterally, as was done with the residential school system, it is going to mean a terrific amount of damage done to native communities.
The Associate Minister is from British Columbia. She is aware today of some of the serious problems that have been caused in native communities because of the residential school system. I suggest that she look at programs that are going on, for example, on the Cowi-chan reserve today and on reserves in the Shuswap area. The residential school system, by taking a whole generation of children away from their parents and their communities, has deprived those children of an understanding of family relationships, of how relationships occur between parents and children. It has contributed to a great deal of child abuse, sexual abuse, suicide on reserves. There is a whole generation of children who have grown up and become parents without a complete understanding of how families operate and interact.
Fortunately we are seeing native social workers who have gone through post-secondary education, native doctors and psychologists, native counsellors who have gone through and understand the system themselves. They are able to counsel and help these people to restore the family relationships that have been broken up by our residential school system. These communities are beginning to see the light at the end of the tunnel

April 24, 1989
Supply
where they can function as normal, healthy communities and families again. A terrific amount of damage has been done by unilateral interpretation of the provisions of the treaty. It is time to sit down with the natives of the treaty nations to develop a formula, a process, a forum for interpreting those treaties that give equal weight to the native view.
I questioned the Minister before on the human rights aspect of this case. Quite apart from the aboriginal rights or treaty rights, there is the human rights aspect of this case. Canada is not internationally acclaimed for the way it treats its minorities. It is not a shining example to other countries because of the way it treats its minorities. As Mr. Yalden referred to in the annual human rights report, the main embarrassment of this country is the way that we treat native Indians.
As I pointed out to the Associate Minister, when you see figures which indicate that 4 per cent of native students participate in post-secondary education, whereas the participation rate for the population as a whole is 27 per cent, it is a clear indication of racial bias in this program. There is a clear obligation on this House to correct that racial bias. How do we do it? We do it as many other countries have done and as this country has done on many occasions: through an affirmative action program. If there is a deficiency, if there is an inequity of participation rate of certain racial groups, that inequity must be eliminated. We have an obligation to do that.
I hear the objections that we do not have the money right now, that these are pretty tough times. I read that line in the Minister's speech last Friday. Well, these are tough times. I recall during the 1984 election campaign the Prime Minister of this country saying that we will go after equality for women when the economy turns around. I want to ask you, Madam Speaker, would Abraham Lincoln have been known as the great liberator if he had said: "We will free the slaves when the economy gets better"? This is unfit business for Canada. When the participation rate of native students is at 4 per cent and the participation rate of the population as a whole is 27 per cent, we have an obligation to redress as quickly as possible that glaring inequity. It is going to be pointed out by people across this country and around the world in describing the way that we treat our native citizens.
The difference here is a racial difference. There is a racial bias in access to post-secondary education in this country. That is something that we are obliged to correct immediately. If we are to retain our stature as a democracy in the western world, we must correct it immediately. You do not correct a problem like this by cutting funding, by limiting funding or even by using words and phrases in Minister's letters which suggest that funding is going to be limited. We know, your Alberta caucus knows, those in the Galleiy know that when you talk about limiting funding, you are talking about reducing the flow of the participation rate of native students. That is precisely what you are talking about. You are talking about slowing down the program. That runs absolutely counter to what we should be doing as a countiy to make this a place that we can be proud of, where we practice racial equality rather than just preach it.
I strongly support the motion that was presented by the Liberal Party. I hope the members of the Alberta caucus of the Conservative Party will vote for it because they have expressed concerns about it. I hope they will be able to convince the balance of the Conservative caucus to support this motion unanimously.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
subtopic: SITTING RESUMED The House resumed at 11.41 a.m.
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I am interested in the rhetoric and history, flawed as it might be, that we were subjected to by the Hon. Member for Comox-Alberni (Mr. Skelly). I must say that I believe the Hon. Member is talking through his hat. I take exception to some of his remarks because I believe they actually promote racism.
Let me point out that this program is one of the most reasonable and responsible in the world. For the Member's information, the funding in Canada for our 15,000 students is about four times what it is in the United States. In the United States, the budget is about $32.9 million for their 15,000 students enrolled in post-secondary education. Here in Canada, that budget is $130 million. Why is the Hon. Member trying to deny that this program is responsible, reasonable and fair?

subtopic: SITTING RESUMED The House resumed at 11.41 a.m.
speechtext:
Because it isn't, Madam Speaker. The Hon. Member compares our program with that in the United States. Maybe it is the goal on the Government side to harmonize our program with the United States. I hope that is not the case.
April 24, 1989

The question is not who does what and who does it better, the question is how much better do we have to do in order to achieve equity? When we are seeking equity in a democratic society, where we have the right of access to post-secondary education on an equal basis, not on a racial basis, we have to spend the money that is necessary to get that equity. That should be the objective.
The objective should not be to cut back access to the program or to delay equity, as the Minister suggested when he said: "Maybe we could talk about this over a 10 year period". People want equity now. People deserve equity now. They have been waiting for 120 years to get equity. Now there is a program in which they have an opportunity to achieve equity. But they know, I think you know, and we know they are not going to get that equity if you cut back on this program. You know it.

speakerposition: Minister of State (Indian Affairs and Northern Development)
subtopic: SITTING RESUMED The House resumed at 11.41 a.m.
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I was very amused by the Hon. Member's comment about harmonizing our policy. I hope he does not do too much damage to his tendons with all that knee-jerking. I suspect there will be a great deal more.
I want to associate myself with his remarks about the effect of the residential schools. I do not think there is any doubt that they have played havoc. While there are native people who say the schools worked for them, they certainly have been a serious impediment to the development of some of the social and familial strengths that native communities require. That is something we can certainly agree upon.
However, I want to comment on his remarks about the role of post-secondary education and the general educational situation. I suggest that our policy is certainly a very strong program of affirmative action. There are no other Canadians who have this assistance from the federal Government for post-secondary education. I reiterate that it is a policy to which the federal Government is deeply committed. The fact that our philosophic underpinning is not that of the treaty nations, that we do not see it as a treaty obligation, does not mean that we do not see it as a vitally important policy and important part of our desire to see native people assume their rightful role in Canadian society.
We must also recognize that when we look at the relative participation rates of native and non-native students in Canada, the difficulty is a reflection of problems before the post-secondary education level.
Supply
When we are dealing with the post-secondary program we are talking about students who have completed high school successfully and have met the entrance requirements for post-secondary institutions. There is another problem in Canada in getting native students to that level. That is not something which is the subject of this particular program. I think it is important to distinguish with regard to that problem, which I agree is serious.
There are initiatives in which the federal Government has been involved. I am grateful to see initiatives on the part of many provincial Governments to try to deal with it directly because it is their level of responsibility. The federal Government contracts with provincial Governments to obtain educational facilities for native students where the bands do not choose to have a band school.
It is a very difficult issue and one should not confuse the two. I certainly share with the Hon. Member a great deal of concern for the extent to which, even now, native students are not getting to that level of preparation. That is a continuing challenge for Canadian society, but not a basis on which to suggest there is a racial bias that is somehow reflected in this program. This program deals with those students who have made it this far. They are a source of great satisfaction to all Canadians.
Yes, their numbers are too small and that is an additional challenge for us, quite aside from this post-secondary program.

subtopic: SITTING RESUMED The House resumed at 11.41 a.m.
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I am not sure if the Minister is admitting that the Government is not putting enough money into education programs at the elementary and secondary level as well, but I would agree with her if she is suggesting that. I hope that in her next meeting with the Minister she can persuade him to make sure more money and more resources are allocated to elementary and secondary education for native Indians as well so that even more people can be qualified to come through this program.
Not all of the complaints of native communities rest with the post-secondary program. A lot of the complaints rest with the elementary and secondary programs where their funding is now being attacked and underfunded by that ministry as well.
There are some serious problems at both ends of the schedule. By referring strictly to post-secondary education funding in this debate, we were only conforming with the motion that was put on the floor. If the Minister wishes to amend the motion so that we can discuss all aspects of Indian education funding, that would open it

April 24, 1989
