up to perhaps four or five more opposition days. We would certainly be prepared to take part in that debate.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
subtopic: SITTING RESUMED The House resumed at 11.41 a.m.
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I want to make a comment regarding some figures that the Hon. Member opposite quoted a few moments ago. He suggested that 27 per cent of all Canadians were enrolled in post-secondary education as opposed to 4 per cent of the native population. My figures are somewhat different. According to Statistics Canada data for 1987-88, 5 per cent of all Canadians are enrolled in post-secondary institutions and 3 per cent of Indians are enrolled in post-secondary institutions. That is a difference of 2 per cent, not 23 per cent as suggested by my hon. colleague opposite.
Second, the Hon. Member spent close to 10 minutes of his speech saying how he felt about treaty rights and so on, but he did not answer the essential question. The essential question is: Does the Hon. Member's Party recognize post-secondary education as a treaty right for Indians?

subtopic: SITTING RESUMED The House resumed at 11.41 a.m.
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I did not consider it an essential question. During my speech I talked about whether our Party agrees with that. There is certainly no question that natives, especially in the treaty areas, believe that post-secondary education is a treaty right, and that is their interpretation of the treaty. The Government, on its side, has said through the words of the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development (Mr. Cadieux), that it is not a treaty right, in his belief.
I said that rather than this Party stating whether it is or isn't, because we have no more right than you to interpret a treaty unilaterally, there should be a forum set up between native nations which have signed treaties with Canada and Canada to work out interpretations of the provisions of the treaties so that those interpretations reflect the circumstances of modern times. That is the position of this Member, and I am certain it would be the position of this Party as well.

subtopic: SITTING RESUMED The House resumed at 11.41 a.m.
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I am very happy to have an opportunity to join in the debate on my Party's motion concerning Indian education because I represent some 12 Indian bands across the
Algoma Manitoulin district right from the Batchawana Band in Sault Ste Marie to the Wikwemikong Band on the eastern end of the Manitoulin Island. I do not think there is any issue on which we have received stronger representation in the last year and a half than the question of Indian post-secondary education.
I do think we have made remarkable progress in many aspects of Indian affairs over the last 15 or 20 years. However, there has been progress made in the field of education. Now a cap is being put on this funding when the problem has always been to provide support for education at the local level for those students who are successful in passing grade 12 or grade 13. It is hard to believe that the Government is capping that funding and capping it in this way.
Last week, chiefs, councillors, students and band members from most of the reserves in the Algoma-Man-itoulin area attended the protest here on Parliament Hill. They were protesting this cap which is discouraging for those students who have been successful in completing grade 12 or grade 13. As well, it is discouraging for the students who are in secondary school. For example, I received a letter just last week from Kelly Esquimaux, a student at the Manitoulin Secondary School and a resident of the Sucker Creek Reserve on Manitoulin Island. She writes:
I am writing to you in regard to the recent aboriginal education assistance cut-backs. I am a high school student at Manitoulin Secondary School and I will be attending college in the fall which means these cut-backs will be affecting me. As MP of my district, I was hoping you would be able to help me and my people fight these cut-backs. Prime Minister Mulroney is being very unfair. An agreement was made and now he is breaking it. Please help us. Thank you. Yours truly, Kelly Esquimaux.
I have received a number of letters like that, letters which portray the uncertainty and concern felt by students in post-secondary education institutions and those in high school at this time as well.
I received a letter from the United Chiefs and Councillors of the Manitoulin district, a district with some six Indian reserves. It is a long letter which outlines the whole problem with the capping of post-secondary education funding. This letter was written to the former Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development. In summary, it reads:
April 24, 1989

We believe the Government is interested in cutting the deficit at the expense of the First Nations education. The Government should look at other means to decrease the deficit problem rather than at the expense of First Nations. Further, we conclude that your department is not committed to the education of First Nations as you previously stated. Mr. Minister, to proceed with your department's present course of action will undoubtedly eliminate forever any hope of establishing a trust relationship which is crucial and fundamental in creating a sound working environment.
That letter is signed by the six Chiefs of the First Nations of Manitoulin District.
This is a very important matter. It is one that cuts right across the entire district that I represent. A letter was sent to me by the social counsellor for the Garden River Indian Band located just outside of Sault Ste Marie. The letter points out that in 1976, when the control was under the Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development, there were only 35 students from the Garden River Band attending high school and that year, there was only one graduate. Today, with the control under the responsibility of the Band Council and its education committee, there are 85 students attending high school in Sault Ste Marie. Usually 10 to 12 students graduate each year and on average, 12 to 14 students start in kindergarten. This speaks of the success Indian bands have been having. However, if 12 to 14 students are entering elementary school and 10 to 12 students are graduating, will that be the end of the road? Will those 12 or 14 students be able to go on to post-secondary institutions?
The letter points out as well that all of the students who graduated in the previous year are employed. These students attended and graduated from Sault College or colleges like Lake Superior State College. These people have been trained as child care workers, law and security people, civil engineers, nurses, business administrators, RNAs, heavy diesel mechanics, finance and sales managers, computer engineers and lab technicians. These people are all employed, and that is the crux of the argument. If the students do not go on to get a complete education which will help them secure jobs, will they be able to enter the workforce? Of course, these are the arguments that were made last week when the Assembly of First Nations held its protest here.
There were other concerns expressed by the Garden River Band social counsellor. She said that her concerns are three-fold. Maintenance rates have been reduced
Supply
for single students and single students with dependants. Tuition assistance for students attending foreign and private institutions has been reduced. The maximum length of assistance has been reduced from 96 student months to 48 student months. She goes on to point out that many of the students from the Garden River Reserve attend Algoma College or Sault College in Sault Ste Marie, but five students are in second year at Lake Superior State College which is just across the river in Sault, Michigan, and two are in their first year. For these students, tuition support will be cut off by up to $900 per year. She points out that already, some students have to supplement their books and supplies by up to $200 in United States funds per year.
I am sure that measure was taken because the Department was thinking that students can get training at the University of Toronto rather than some university in the United States and why should we pay for that additional tuition. However, the practical results are that students in Sault Ste Marie, rather than being able to commute back and forth to Lake Superior State College in Sault, Michigan, will not be able to do so because of the cut-backs in funding of tuition and supplies for those attending foreign colleges.
These are some of the concerns which are being expressed to me and I hope that the Government will be prepared to lift the cap that has been proposed on post-secondary education. It should be left the way it has been in the past. A notional amount has been put in the Estimates and if the number of students applying for assistance were to go beyond that, the Department would go back to the Treasury Board to get additional funds. We are talking here about the future of literally thousands of students who have grown up with the least opportunities. Those who have struggled through the system and graduated from high school to prepare themselves to go on to university should not be denied that opportunity. I do not know the exact numbers. I am told that something in the range of 2,000 would qualify. If they qualify, it is not a cost to the Government now, but rather an investment in the future to ensure that these students will have a productive job and a productive lifestyle and will not be a burden on the state in the years to come because they have been able to receive that extra training at college or university.

April 24, 1989
I hope that the Government recognizes the wisdom in the recommendation in the statement which is before the House today, and puts a moratorium on the capping of the budget for post-secondary education. In the long run not only will the Government be doing the best thing, but it will be doing the proper thing for these students who will not be denied an opportunity to go on and take post-secondary education, not only this fall but in the years ahead.
With your permission, Madam Speaker, I will call it one o'clock.

ARMENIA
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I would like to remind the House that today, April 24, is the seventy-fourth anniversary of the first genocide of the twentieth century, when 1,500,000 Armenians were massacred by the Turkish-Ottoman Governments between 1915 and 1922. subtopic: CONTRIBUTION OF ARMENIANS
CONTRIBUTION OF ARMENIANS
speechtext:
In the course of my work I am always struck that people of many and diverse origins view Canada as a land of opportunity and Canadians as a people who are committed to freedom and democracy. Most important, we are seen as a county whose strength and vitality have their roots in Canada's multicultural reality. Canada is a home to people, cultures and traditions from around the world.
Many Canadians, including those of Armenian origin, came to this country to escape injustice. They have made a valued contribution to the political, social and economic fabric of Canada.
Today as our Armenian Canadians commemorate tragic events, including the 1915 genocide experienced elsewhere, we salute their efforts as Canadians, to ensure that future generations are spared the denial of human rights they suffered in other countries, in other times. Together we are working to shape a nation that is strong, self-confident and caring, a nation that looks forward to an even brighter and more promising future for all of us who live together in our unique and multicultural traditions.
April 24, 1989

subtopic: EXPANSION OF HOME-BUYING OPPORTUNITIES
EXPANSION OF HOME-BUYING OPPORTUNITIES
speechtext:
The budgetary constraints in which the Government finds itself call for innovative ways to alleviate the housing crisis in Canada. One of the ways this could be done is to allow the use of retirement funds for home purchases. Under current regulations, many low, and middle-income first time buyers are denied access to RRSP funds for home purchases, while individuals with large RRSP holdings are able to make this kind of investment. By relaxing the barriers which prevent the investment of less than $25,000 in RRSP money in a principal residence, including eliminating insurance requirements on retirement- based mortgages, we can give home buying opportunities to many more young families. Expanding regulations that allow the investment of employer contributing or administered pension plans would also serve to open up a very tight housing market. Allowing Canadians to invest in their own futures is a sound idea, one that would not require any additional tax expenditures. This makes the plan preferable to RHOSPs or other tax deferred plans. This
is a bold idea, but it is a new idea we will have to explore in order to solve the present housing crunch.

subtopic: FUNDING OF REAL WOMEN'S ORGANIZATION
FUNDING OF REAL WOMEN'S ORGANIZATION
speechtext:
This past weekend the Government sponsored a conference for REAL Women. The Secretary of State (Mr. Weiner) has said that this group meets the women's program criteria for funding.
The criteria do not include bashing the female Supreme Court Justices. They do not include spreading lies and hatred about lesbians and gays. They do not include absolutely ridiculous seminars on how children in day care will all become psychopaths. It does not include raving about pre-marital sex.
The criteria do state that the project should deal with how barriers to women's equality should be addressed. This conference denied that any barriers exist.
Women's program officials have told equality seeking women's groups that their funding could be cut by up to 65 per cent in the coming budget.
This Government is funding anti-child care, anti-employment equity groups, and cutting back on equalityseeking women's groups. This clearly represents the Government's true agenda for women. It is a back-to-the-kitchen agenda.

(Wish all my heart, I am with you!)
April 24, 1989

subtopic: VALDEZ OIL SPILL
VALDEZ OIL SPILL
speechtext:
In the April 8 issue of The Economist, you will find the following on the Exxon Valdez oil spill:
Do not be taken in by oil company promises that opening the Arctic National Wildlife Refuge to oil exploration will never harm the 170,000 cariboo that go there to calve. Oil deserves to be found and pumped out if, and only if, it can be sold at a price that covers the cost of appropriate environmental safeguards, by a company with a powerful incentive to keep those safeguards working.
Modem business diffuses personal responsibility too rapidly. If you fine an oil-spilling company 10 times the value of the spilt oil, its insurance rates merely go up. Directors and employees of companies which profit from things that are very unlikely to turn very unpleasant should be personally exposed to fear of these unpleasantnesses. They should lose their jobs when the 'impossible' happens just as the president of Japan Airlines quit when an aging jet crashed. That sense of personal responsibility would do much to keep the safety drills slick, the captain sober, the otters swimming.
Even The Economist is turning green!

subtopic: CALL FOR INDEPENDENCE
CALL FOR INDEPENDENCE
speechtext: It is now 74 years since the horrific genocide in 1915, when at least 1.5 million Armenians were massacred. Armenians in Canada, and in other countries around the world, are still waiting for Governments to officially recognize that the genocide did, indeed, occur. In February, 1988 over 30 Armenians were killed while peacefully demonstrating in the City of Sumgait. Last month I visited Soviet Armenia to talk to Armenians who survived the devastating earthquake which occurred on December 7, 1988. Between 50,000 and 100,000 Armenians lost their lives as a result of this earthquake. Despite these historic tragedies, Armenians around the world continue to dream of a free and independent Armenia. Nothing will deter Armenians from this dream of rebirth. Nothing will crush their spirits or their souls.

subtopic: CALL FOR RECOGNITION OF ARMENIAN GENOCIDE
CALL FOR RECOGNITION OF ARMENIAN GENOCIDE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, today marks the commemoration of the seventy-fourth anniversary of the Armenian genocide as the Hon. Member just noted.
In the period of 1915 to 1923 over one million Armenians were killed and millions of others were driven from their homeland by the Turkish-Ottoman Governments. This certainly represents one of the saddest chapters in the history of the 20th century.
The international community has often been slow to recognize such realities and Canadian Governments over the years have been no different. The time has come for the Canadian Government to recognize and condemn the Armenian genocide, to urge the Government of Turkey to do likewise and to provide redress to the Armenian community.
I know that I join with many other Canadians in noting the importance of recognizing the Armenian genocide and other events, both past and present, in which minority peoples are oppressed and persecuted. To remember such things, as Canada should in a regular way on April 24, is to keep hope alive that some day the earth will be rid of such injustices.

subtopic: POSSIBLE RAIL LINE ABANDONMENT ON P.E.I.
POSSIBLE RAIL LINE ABANDONMENT ON P.E.I.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, once again the Prince Edward Island way of life has been threatened by the federal Government. As we speak, hearings regarding railway abandonment on Prince Edward Island are taking place in Charlottetown. This time it is the operations at the Kensington and Borden subdivisions that are being threatened.

The provincial Government cannot afford to complete this task, especially with all of the cut-backs that we hear will be announced in Thursday's Budget speech.
April 24, 1989

What about the employees and their families who will be affected? Many have lived and raised their families on P.E.I. for many years. They have given the better part of their lives to CN, but the compensation package they will receive from CN is grossly inadequate.
Given this, I call on the Government to ensure that the province is adequately compensated and that the affected employees and their families will be taken care of by CN.

Mr. Speaker, this week is National Organ Donor Awareness Week. The Department of National Health and Welfare is joining professional and voluntary health organizations in activities to heighten public and health professional awareness of the benefits of organ and tissue donation and transplantation.
Families are encouraged to discuss and make a decision about organ donation before a tragedy occurs. Health professionals are urged to examine how they may participate in the organ donation process.
You are invited to consider organ donation and to sign a donor card or the consent portion of your driver's licence if you have not already done so. Discuss your decision with family, friends, constituents and professional colleagues and ask them to follow your example. By doing so you will be giving or encouraging others to give the most precious gift of all, the gift of life.

subtopic: INDEXATION OF CN AND CP PENSIONS
INDEXATION OF CN AND CP PENSIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Canadian Pacific Pensioners National Council held their annual convention this past Friday here in Ottawa. This organization represents CP pensioners from across the country. The focus of this year's meeting was the plight that many of the CP pensioners are in. This plight of the CP pensioners, which is very similar to the problems of the CN pensioners, is due in large part to their having no adequate indexation of their pensions. Because of this there are CP and CN pensioners across the country living in poverty.
How can this Government allow this to happen when these Canadians have contributed so much to the building of this nation? Surely this Government, which pays so much attention to enlarging or ensuring the large profits of major corporations, can also ensure that pensioners receive adequate indexation of their pensions. I call upon the Government to act quickly on behalf of CP and CN pensioners to right this wrong.

subtopic: RECOGNITION OF ARMENIAN GENOCIDE URGED
RECOGNITION OF ARMENIAN GENOCIDE URGED
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it was a pleasure for me together with my Liberal colleagues and, indeed, Members from all sides of the House, to gather at 12.30 p.m. at the foot of this great parliamentary institution to join with 2,000 Canadians of Armenian descent. They are here not only to remind us of the purge of the evil, the genocide, that happened to their brothers and sisters some 74 years ago, but also to be vigilant, to send forth a message from Parliament Hill to reach all corners of the world where human rights and human dignity are stepped on, that at least Canada, morally and ethically, will stand up to say that that is wrong and that it recognizes it. Two thousand people were outside. There were 2,000 people last year and the year before, but we need to go further than simply having those people come to our institution to remind us to recognize it.
I believe, Mr. Speaker, that there is an emerging consensus on all sides of the House for this Parliament to stand up and boldly recognize an evil for what it was. I believe there is a consensus to have the Secretary of State for External Affairs Minister (Mr. Clark) and this Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) move on the promise that they made in 1984 to move through the United Nations and mobilize international leadership and international opinion, because it is not weakness to recognize what has happened, it is strength.
I urge this Government to pick up the pieces and to coalesce the emerging feeling that all Members share on this issue. Let us stand up. Let us pass a resolution through the House of Commons and let that set the tone and example for other Governments and other countries around the globe.

April 24, 1989

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am prepared to take the Deputy Prime Minister at his word. Indeed, the election should be over and it is back to business, to use the Deputy Prime Minister's words,"as usual".
During last fall's federal electoral effort the Prime Minister said: "Our promises are all within Michael Wilson's fiscal framework. Every nickel has been accounted for." In January, after that said electoral effort, the Prime Minister said: "We are expecting difficulty on the fiscal side."
I want to ask the Deputy Prime Minister today whether or not the Government of Canada stands behind the $17 billion in promises made both before and during the federal election campaign.
Specifically, will the Deputy Prime Minister tell the House today, and through the House the people of Newfoundland and Labrador, that the Government of Canada stands behind the Hibernia agreement announced last July in St. Johns, Newfoundland, by the Prime Minister of Canada and by the former Premier of Newfoundland and Labrador? Will he give us the assurance today that it is business as usual?
April 24, 1989

Members, and to all the citizens of Newfoundland and Labrador that the Hibernia project was a project and that is a project which the Government believes is important, both for the national interest as well as for Newfoundland and Labrador. subtopic: REQUEST FOR FEDERAL REASSURANCE

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I get awfully worried when I hear a Minister say the Hibernia project "was a project that is a project," and was a project that we are standing behind. It frightens the daylights out of me.
Let me put my question clearly. Last July, in St. Johns, Newfoundland, the Prime Minister of Canada, the Premier of Newfoundland, and the Minister representing Newfoundland in the federal Cabinet, announced that the Hibernia deal was done, the Hibernia project was going to go ahead, the federal Government was putting the federal Treasury behind the project, and that a legally binding agreement would be signed by March 31. It is now April 24 and there is no legally binding agreement.
I ask the Minister of Energy again, will he stand in the House today and say, days in advance of the federal Budget, that the Hibernia project is a go, that the federal Government is not backing away, and that the Government is prepared to sit down to discuss with the new Liberal Government in Newfoundland the details of that project, including the royalty regime for Newfoundland which is one of the worst in Canada's history?

subtopic: THE ECONOMY
THE ECONOMY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Finance. On the weekend in Ottawa the Minister was threatening once again to impose a Conservative view of fairness on the whole of the country when he said that in the coming Budget, when it comes to tax increases and cut-backs in programs, Canadians could expect the Government to be fair.
Considering that he said the same thing in 1984, not long before he brought in his subsequent Budget, a Budget that increased taxes on the poor by 60 per cent, increased taxes on the average family by 17 per cent, and reduced taxes on the rich by 6 per cent, will the Minister of Finance guarantee Canadians that Thursday's Budget will not be a repetition of that concept of fairness?

subtopic: THE ECONOMY
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subtopic: THE ECONOMY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think the Hon. Member is referring to comments that I made on a television program over the weekend wherein I was making the observation that the federal Government debt is at very high levels and that the problem must be addressed. I would expect that he also would agree that it must be addressed. It is not a partisan issue. It is not an ideological issue. It is pure arithmetic that leads to the obvious conclusion that something must be done about it.
April 24, 1989

On that same program I made the point that we are going to be very sensitive to the ability of people to support that effort of getting the deficit down. We would expect that the broad range of economic policies, including getting control of the government debt, will lead to the same sort of economic performance that we had over the last four years, which the Hon. Member continues to ignore, yet there it is staring him right in the face.
Some 1.5 million jobs were created since September, 1984. That is the program that we want to continue over the next four years.

subtopic: INTEREST RATE INCREASES
INTEREST RATE INCREASES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Government has sanctioned, because it has done nothing to the contrary, the continual increases in the interest rates that the Bank of Canada has imposed on the people of Canada. The last time we saw this kind of steady escalation, as the Minister will recall when he was on this side of the House, was the early eighties which led to the most serious recession in Canada in the post-war period.
Since the Government has stood back, watched and actually supported this action by the Bank of Canada, does the Minister not at least fear that his Budget, which he has said is going to provide us with tax increases and program cuts, combined with a high interest rate policy, could be just enough to tip this country into a serious recession once again?

subtopic: INTEREST RATE INCREASES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we are not as a country in a position where we can ignore the debt problem that has grown up over the past 20 years. It is something that must be dealt with.
The Hon. Member refers to the interest rate problem. He is pointing to a symptom of the problem, not the cause of the problem. The cause of the problem is inflation and an economy that is growing faster than the capacity of the economy to handle.
What we would expect as a result of this Budget is that we would put a better balance between the monetary policy of the Bank of Canada and the fiscal policy of the Government of Canada so that we can see some opportunity for interest rates to come down. That is the objective that we are following in this Budget.
Oral Questions

We on this side of the House have the sense to learn from past mistakes so we can avoid the problems of 1982.

subtopic: HOUSING
HOUSING
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of State for Housing. Today Canadians are dismayed about whether the Minister's priorities have changed since he became Minister. In a Toronto newspaper today, the Minister made the outrageous statement that Canadians can no longer assume that 30 per cent of their income will get them reasonable accommodation.
It was not long ago that the Minister could be counted on as someone who was willing to stand up for the Canadian dream of owning a home. Now it turns out that the Minister will be remembered as the person who sold it out.
My question is this. Why is the Minister now telling Canadians that they have to abandon the great national dream of owning their own home unless they are prepared to pay more than 30 per cent of their income towards the cost of putting a roof over their heads? Doesn't this Government have any heart left?

subtopic: HOUSING
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I know the Hon. Member has been reading the newspapers. I hope that he will try to read them a little more carefully than he appears to have done this time. Certainly no one is telling the Canadian people that the dream of owning a home has come to an end, certainly not me and certainly not the Government. Our goal is to try to make sure that every Canadian does have a roof over his or her head and a roof that is affordable to them.
April 24, 1989

The indication that the Hon. Member refers to in the press today was aimed at just dealing with the facts of life as they are in the country at the moment. Many, many people, as the Hon. Member knows, pay more than 30 per cent of their income towards the cost of housing. I want that to come down. So does the Government. That is what we are aiming to try our best to do.

subtopic: HOUSING CO-OPERATIVES
HOUSING CO-OPERATIVES
speechtext:
The reality of the situation is this. Does the Minister not know that people in Vancouver, in Toronto, in London and other cities across this great country have to go to food banks because more than half of their total income has to go towards rents?
The Minister says that everybody is getting squeezed by the Budget. If the poorest people in this country are squeezed any harder they will not stand a chance of ever getting back on their feet. Will the Government fight the deficit solely on the backs of the poor?
Does the Minister plan to cut housing co-operatives and social projects, and leave the families who live in them to fend for themselves?

subtopic: HOUSING CO-OPERATIVES

I can assure the Hon. Member that this Government and this Minister will do everything they possibly can to assist Canadians to have housing that is affordable to them.

THE ECONOMY
subsubtopic: REQUEST THAT BANK OF CANADA ROLL BACK INTEREST RATES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of Finance. I am sure you are aware, like everyone in the country, that the Budget on Thursday will bring about tax increases and program cuts for ordinary Canadians.
Oral Questions
Since interest rates in this country are now more than 3 per cent higher than those in the United States, instead of raising taxes for ordinary people and cutting back on programs for ordinary people, when will the Minister tell the Governor of the Bank of Canada, John Crow, that the time has come to roll back interest rates so they are at least on a level that is near the rate in the United States?

subtopic: THE ECONOMY
subsubtopic: REQUEST THAT BANK OF CANADA ROLL BACK INTEREST RATES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think the Hon. Member is getting quite selective. If he looks at the market rates of interest he will see that they are in the 2 per cent to 2-1/4 per cent range, not the 3 per cent range he has indicated.
The substance of his question is that the Governor of the Bank of Canada should just roll back interest rates. I ask him to consider how the Governor of the Bank of Canada would do that. The way I suggest he would do that is to print money. We all know that printing money leads to inflation, more inflation leads to higher interest rates, and that is exactly what we are trying to avoid.
We are trying to avoid the problems we got into in 1981 and 1982 when inflation ran at 13 per cent and led to 22 per cent and 23 per cent interest rates at the time.
Surely the Hon. Member would like us to learn from mistakes of the past.

If the Hon. Member wants to go back and look at what the consensus of private sector forecasters has been over the same four-year period, recognizing that forecasts are

made for the future and are sometimes hard to predict, the record of this Government is better than the consensus of private sector forecasters during the four years we have been in office.

subtopic: TAXATION
TAXATION
subsubtopic: PROPOSED NATIONAL SALES TAX-ROLE OF PROVINCES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of Finance. Without the co-operation of his provincial counterparts, a fair and equitable national sales tax may never see the light of the day. Some Premiers have been highly critical of a national sales tax program.
I understand that the Minister met with his provincial colleagues recently. Could he tell us if he has made any progress? Will he have the co-operation to ensure that all Canadians will be part of a fair national sales tax?

subtopic: TAXATION
subsubtopic: PROPOSED NATIONAL SALES TAX-ROLE OF PROVINCES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as the Hon. Member knows, a national sales tax is quite a complex undertaking. As he said, we have had consultations with the Finance Ministers of the provinces for about two years now. We have thoroughly assessed the issues that are exposed in the analysis of a national sales tax.
I think there is a veiy clear understanding of the urgent need for the federal Government to reform the federal sales tax a hidden tax which is very destructive in the economy today.
I have tried to assess the urgency, the commitment of the provinces to changing their sales tax and I have to say that at this point in time I think a national sales tax is out of reach. However, I do believe that it is essential that the federal Government move ahead with its sales tax reforms so I have advised my colleagues in the provincial Governments this morning of our desire to proceed with federal sales tax reform and acknowledged the very great commitment that they made to the national sales tax objective. Unfortunately, however, that is out of reach at this point in time.

subtopic: SOFTWOOD LUMBER EXPORT TAX
SOFTWOOD LUMBER EXPORT TAX
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in the absence of the Minister for International Trade I will direct my question to the Secretary of State for External Affairs. It concerns the softwood lumber export tax.
Last Friday afternoon the G.W. Martin Company in Sault Ste. Marie and Searchmont laid off some 300 workers, and another couple of hundred are being laid off in the bush operations. This brings to over 1,300 the number of workers who have been laid off since the Government imposed the export tax on January 1, 1987. This company complained that it had spent over $1 million on export tax and was shutting down because of losses in the operation of these two mills.
Can the Minister tell these laid-off workers exactly what action the Government plans to take to provide some relief to them for the loss of jobs and the losses to the communities throughout northern Ontario?

subtopic: SOFTWOOD LUMBER EXPORT TAX
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, everyone is aware of the critical situation in which the solid wood producers find themselves in the present circumstances, particularly here in Ontario.
There are a number of factors, only one of which concerns the softwood lumber tax. There is no doubt that the Province of Ontario, which has benefited from this tax immensely, has flexibility that, if properly managed, could offer some relief to those who are the worst affected. An industry that is investing in the current year roughly $6 billion in expansion, that is the industry in total, is hardly one that is in dire straits.

subtopic: SOFTWOOD LUMBER EXPORT TAX
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I can assure you that these employees who have been laid off are in dire straits, as are many other workers in northern Ontario.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, why does the Government of Canada steadfastly refuse to renegotiate and eliminate this export tax? There is a solid provision in the Memorandum of Understanding, under Section 8, to renegotiate the tax if circumstances have changed. Clearly, circumstances have changed in northern Ontario. Companies are going broke, workers are being laid off, plants are being shut down, and whole communities are being shut down because of this tax.
April 24, 1989

Surely that is reason enough to go to the Americans to renegotiate this? If they refuse, then there is provision under Section 9 of the agreement to do away with the tax unilaterally. I think it is about time the Government did one or the other.

subtopic: REQUEST THAT TAX AGREEMENT BE RENEGOTIATED

Mr. Speaker, my hon. friend demonstrates knowledge of the provisions in the Memorandum of Understanding. As soon as the provinces have taken measures to offset the tax, as every province has done in Canada except Ontario, we will have a basis for negotiating out of the agreement.
If he wants to help his constituents in northern Ontario, perhaps he ought to make a trip to Queen's Park, as I have advised him to do, to encourage the Government there to do what every province has done, and put us on a basis to permit us to get out of this agreement.

Since September of 1984, Chinese Canadians in my riding of Hamilton West as well as those in ridings throughout Canada have been pleading for a bipartisan parliamentary resolution for an apology from the Government, acknowledging the injustice and the appropriate remedial action to be taken by the Government over the head tax and the Exclusion Act forced on Chinese immigrants early in the century.

MINISTER'S POSITION
speechtext:

subtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 81-POST-SECONDARY EDUCATION FUNDING-NATIVE PEOPLES

speechtext:
The House resumed consideration of the motion of Mr. Nault:
That this House recognize that the Government's arbitrary and misanthropic policy of unilaterally capping future funding for postsecondary education for Canada's native peoples severely undermines the right and efforts of these peoples to enhance their capacity to make meaningful and lasting improvements to their economic and social conditions and to establish their self-reliance, thereby condemning them to unacceptable living conditions and driving them to desperate measures; and
That this House urge the Government to terminate its plans to cap this funding and to take steps to establish effective bilateral consultations on this and other matters vital to the improvement of the lives of and the ending of discrimination toward these Native peoples.

subtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 81-POST-SECONDARY EDUCATION FUNDING-NATIVE PEOPLES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to have the opportunity to speak to the issue before us, which is a most important one.
I would like to remind Members of the House that my riding of Regina-Wascana is the home of Canada's first fully accredited Indian university, named the Saskatchewan Indian Federated College. It is affiliated with the campus of the University of Regina.
The school population has virtually exploded in recent years, to our benefit. Currently there are expansion plans, and I have not heard that this position has been withdrawn. Given the tenor of the current debate before us, my wish is that this goal will soon come true, and I assure them that I will work toward that goal with them as best I can.
In March the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development (Mr. Cadieux) introduced a new policy for native students attending post-secondary institutions. Without question this program is the fairest and most generous of its kind in the world. It is a responsible program, and that is why I am pleased to address the subject.
Federal funding for post-secondary education has increased dramatically over the past decade, which has been alluded to by Members on both sides of the House. Let us not forget that there has been a dramatic increase
in the funding. In 1977-78 when the previous E-12 program was first adopted, the federal Government provided approximately $2,600 per capita in assistance to approximately 3,500 Indian students. In 1988-89 the budget for the program was close to $130 million, and provided close to $9,000 per year to each of some 15,000 students.
The Government's Post-secondary Student Assistance Program is among the most generous in the world, and it is a significant improvement over the provisions of the previous E-12 program. I defy anyone to show us a program that is more generous.
The objective of the new policy is to help Indian and Inuit students gain access to a post-secondary education in order that they can pursue individual careers and contribute to the achievement of Indian self-government and self-reliance while building a better Canada.
I would like to take some time to explain the benefits available to eligible students. Tuition assistance is provided to eligible full-time and part-time students. This category of benefits includes students' fees for registration, tuition, and the cost of books and supplies required for a particular course of studies. In other words, if a science student is required to have a lab coat, that coat would be an eligible expense. If an economics major is required to have a calculator, the program would cover the cost of the calculator.
In addition to tuition assistance, full-time students who are required to live away from their permanent place of residence may receive a wide range of benefits. For example, they may qualify for a travel grant to return to their home once every semester for themselves and any dependants who reside with them. I see little restriction in this policy. These students are also eligible to receive allowances to help cover their living expenses of food, rent, heat, hydro, day care, and other related expenses. In areas where rental costs are higher than normal, Indian students with two or more dependants may receive a special rent supplement.
Beginning in the next academic year single students may receive a maximum monthly living allowance of $675. A married student with an employed spouse and three dependants will receive a maximum of $1,205 per month. A single parent with three dependants will receive a maximum of $1,355 per month, plus a rental supplement where applicable.
April 24, 1989

It is true that under the new program some students may experience a decline in the level of assistance that they receive. I would like to stress that the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development has already made it clear that Indian administering organizations will be given significant latitude in dealing with the special needs of these students. Students will be eligible for post-secondary assistance for the official length of the program that they are pursuing. For example, if they are studying for a medical degree they will be assisted for the full length of the course of study. The program also provides for an additional year of government assistance where it is justified.
It is true that the federal Government will no longer fund students permanently, regardless of their progress. The new policy also enables administering organizations to offer special incentives to eligible students. For example, academic achievement scholarships of up to $1,000 may be awarded to community college, CEGEP and undergraduate students who maintain an average of B or higher.
Undergraduate students may also be eligible for strategic studies scholarships which may be worth up to $3,500, to encourage students to pursue courses of study that will directly contribute to achieving self-government and economic self-reliance.
Incentives are available for full-time students enrolled in an advanced or professional degree program such as a Master's or a doctoral program. These students are eligible for a one-time contribution of up to $1,500.
Despite the significant range of levels of assistance available to Indian post-secondary students, some would argue that that is not enough. These people want the federal Government to guarantee individual natives a free post-secondary education. They want the federal Government to fund each individual for as long as it takes. Unfortunately, that is not a realistic situation.
I can think of no other group in Canadian society that has access to such a focused generous program, nor can I identify a group that is as needful for this type of assistance. Education will open the door to a more fulfilling future for Canada's Indians. We have a social obligation to contribute to that progress.

and to take specific courses defined by the Government, a program in which the students themselves argue they have no input.

subtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 81-POST-SECONDARY EDUCATION FUNDING-NATIVE PEOPLES
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I take this question with a certain degree of pleasure in that it does have a tendency to remove these clouds of suspicion, at least to those who are listening to the Government policy. The clouds of suspicion, of course, have been placed there appropriately by the Opposition-appropriately at least in their minds-and from our position, of course, are certainly not justified.
To get to the meat of the question, there are four points I want to make very clear to this House, to members of the Opposition and to Canadians generally. Students, of course, are free to attend the university of their choice and to take whatever course of study they wish, a freedom I would suggest that has yet to stand the test of equality anywhere else. They can do this without any restriction on the living allowances to which they are entitled provided they are within the over-all limits stated in the policy. Canadians, of course, charge us with the responsibility of making sure that the policies we provide have some sense to them.
The policy states that tuition support and travel allowances will be limited to the costs at the nearest university offering the course of study comparable to the one chosen by the student. I think that is fair. Incentive grants are provided to students who choose to enrol in some specific courses, but again we emphasize that students are not obliged to take these courses.

Madam Speaker, on Friday in the House I brought to the attention of Hon. Members the case of a young native boy, the adopted son of two non-native parents. His parents are desperately seeking financial help to provide the residential treatment their son needs for severe emotional and behavioural problems. Some Members opposite insisted on casting the issue as an educational one, and that is why I am returning to it.
This is not an educational issue, an issue which is the responsibility of the province or of the local school boards. It is rather a question of health care and equal access for native children to care and to opportunities. The boy suffers from foetal alcohol syndrome, a medical condition which affects native children disproportionately and results in severe problems. The condition leads to erratic and violent behaviour. This boy has been professionally diagnosed several times as needing residential treatment.
Funding could be available through the province if the child were not a status Indian. His parents then could enter into an agreement to allow the Children's Aid Society to take over the care of their child and he would get the residential treatment and the help needed for his medical problem. But that cannot happen because the minute his parents do that the Children's Aid Society is obliged to consult with the band from which the boy came. The parents jeopardize their custody of the child to provide the care he needs for his medical problems.

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I would begin by stating something that I mentioned to the Minister on Friday. I appreciate the sentiment with which his statements were made. I sensed a distinct desire on his part to find a resolution to this situation, and a sympathy and sincerity in dealing with that. I much appreciated that. There is, though, still much left to be resolved.
I want to make mention of a couple of comments from across the country. In my City of Saskatoon, the Star Phoenix, not known for its agreement with my Party, said today:
It is high time Indian Affairs Minister Pierre Cadieux relented on his stubborn refusal to negotiate a better deal for Indian postsecondary students and stopped making deceptive statements about universal access. The logic is overwhelming.
The editorial went on:
Beyond honouring a treaty obligation, the investment in Indian post-secondary education promises to pay dividends in reduced welfare and prison costs in the future, to say nothing of the positive contributions native doctors, lawyers, teachers, scientists, etc.,will make to Canadian society.
With so much at stake, it is understandable the native community is fighting to resist funding ceilings which amount to quotas, living allowances cuts which will effectively rule out university attendance for many of them and performance demands which almost guarantee failure. The sooner Cadieux admits the short-sightedness of his department's money-saving tactic, the better for all Canadians.

April 24, 1989
Supply
As we have seen, unlike the rather unimaginative editorial in the Globe and Mail last week, Peter Deba-rats made some similar comments. I do not want to continue with the litany of problems with the Indian population and the circumstances in which they find themselves. We have heard that on a number of occasions in this debate. I think it is important that they be stated, but I would like to go on to point out some concerns with the guidelines.
The Government side has consistently said that these guidelines are better than the old E-12 guidelines. I would like to challenge that. It is not only Indians who question that these guidelines are better. I think the terminology and the facts speak for themselves.
The original E-12 guidelines were also problematic, and going back to them will not solve an enormous amount. At least they are better than these new guidelines which were adopted without effective consultation, and they should not be produced before that appropriate consultation. The original E-12 guidelines were also not subject to satisfactory consultation. They also were deemed to be undesirable by native students and native leaders.
In 1987, the former Minister of Indian Affairs made the matter worse and set the tone for these guidelines by essentially capping those funds, setting priorities for selecting students, placing a 12-month Canadian residency requirement, and removing half salary allowances for graduate students. These changes were made without effective consultation with native leaders. The present guidelines proposed by the Minister also were introduced without effective consultation. None of the 560-odd organizations and individuals consulted on these guidelines were in agreement with the changes.
I will just state what I see as the problems with the changes, and then ask two or three questions. The old E-12 guidelines provide that training and living allowance "shall be" provided. The changes in the new guidelines introduced the terminology "may". Special shelter allowance was available under the E-12 guidelines under certain circumstances. There is no allowance for that under the new guidelines. Tuition allowance, the previous guidelines point out that full fees "shall be paid". Under the new guidelines we have the terminology full fees "may" be paid. Under the old guidelines books and supplies "will" be paid "in full". In the new guidelines, moneys "may" be provided "toward" the cost. Students "shall receive "in full" travel allowance, under the old guidelines. They "may" qualify for a travel grant under the new guidelines.
There are a number of other indications of movements away from the old E-12 guidelines to a less desirable standard under the new ones. We have an increase in the global amount available to students. There had been no increase prior to these introduced changes on April 1 since the introduction of the first E-12 guidelines. A small increase of 6 or 7 per cent does not make up for the cost of living increase over time from the beginning of the previous guidelines to the introduction of these new guidelines, of something approaching 30 per cent.
In real terms, the new guidelines do not add anything very significant to the pockets of Indian students. Indeed, because of some allowance they were entitled to before, which they will now not be entitled to but may receive, they may in fact end up with less. Computations made by Indian groups indicate that almost all of the categories of students receiving assistance under the guidelines will in fact receive in total less under these guidelines than under the old guidelines. There is a movement away from seeing the moneys available as of right to the students to discretionary moneys available under certain circumstances. The terminology "may" is introduced in most of these new guidelines.
Rather than continue the rhetoric, I would like to pose three questions to the Minister. I do not expect him to answer them today, but I think it does suggest that the problems which these new guidelines give rise to. He said there is no cap on the guidelines. He said that there is no monetary limit available for financing post-secondary education students. The program just must work within a budget. Let me pose this question: Supposing, instead of the 15,000 students now who are now applying for money, 15,050 apply for the money, and there is only enough money for 15,000. Is the Government committed to ensuring that the funding will be available to provide for those other 50 students? If they are not committed to ensuring that funding will be available for those other 50 students, quite clearly there is a cap on the program.
With regard to Bill C-31, adding members to band lists, with regard to the demographics of the Indian population, 25 per cent being under 18, 50 per cent being under 25, as well as the backlog from those who did not make it through the previous education system, I wonder what steps the Minister and the Government are making to ensure that the required funding will be available once all of the students reach university and other post-secondary institutions. I think the question remains. Will the Government commit itself to ensuring that no Indian student wanting post-secondary education and qualified to undertake it will be denied the funding to do so? I
April 24, 1989

think we still do not have an appropriate answer to that question.
There is much more to be done with regard to ensuring that these guidelines are appropriate and acceptable to the Indian population, to Indian students and leaders. That has not been done to date. There has not been effective consultation. We must ensure that that takes place. We must ensure that issues which separate the Government and Indian leaders are debated and resolved in the appropriate fashion.
To that end, I would like to move an amendment to the Motion which is on the floor. I move:
Thai the motion be amended by deleting all the words following "desperate measures" and substituting the following therefor:
"That this House call upon the Government to put a moratorium on the implementation of its amended post-secondary education policy for native students while the Government enters into bilateral negotiations with elected representatives of Canada's native peoples".

subtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 81-POST-SECONDARY EDUCATION FUNDING-NATIVE PEOPLES
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I am happy to participate today in this debate. I am truly saddened by the political use of the situation, something which I feel to be very serious. This is a situation which is fraught with misunderstandings. In my view, the emotions on both sides of the issue have gotten out of control and are at a point where people are not listening to what others are saying.
First, I would like to say something about the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development (Mr. Ca-dieux). I have worked with this gentleman over the past four or five years in another portfolio and, indeed, in the present portfolio which he holds. I find him to be an honourable gentleman, one who speaks straight and calls it as he sees it. He tries his hardest to listen to the other person's point of view.

April 24, 1989
Supply
I have had countless meetings with him since this issue came to the fore in the last two to three weeks. I want to say that I have found his comments to be helpful. In my discussions with him I found that he was there to listen.
I also went over and visited with the students who are participating in this hunger strike or fast. I found that a great deal of emotion exists. I tried my hardest to make them understand that there are two sides to the issue. I thought that there really was a possibility that the students could sit down with the Minister upon stopping their hunger strike.
Basically, the students are demanding four things. First, they have said that they would like a moratorium set in place for a year on the issue of the new guidelines and before the new policy comes into effect on September 1. Second, they have said that they want to negotiate the capping or the cut-back in funding. Third, they want to have a bilateral process between the students and the Minister or the Minister's staff to try to work something out that would be suitable to all. Fourth, they would like to see a national student organization established.
I would like to go over these issues point by point. I think it is unfortunate that Members in the House either purposely or inadvertently are distorting the issues and really clouding what is happening. Let us look at the removing of the cap. Somehow during the debate that has somehow evolved into a cut-back.
The Ministry of Indian Affairs had to set up a budget last year so that the Department could take to Treasury Board a realistic budget stating how much money the Department is going to spend over the next year. All Members should recognize that any time a Minister is responsible for a department, he surely has to put in place a budget. Surely he has to say,"This is how much we have to set aside, President of the Treasury Board. This is how much we have to set aside for this specific activity."
For 1987-88, with the best available information the Department had at that time, it submitted a budget. Unfortunately, there was a shortfall affecting 899 students of which 137 were Bill C-31. This was a combination of regionally administered and band administered post-secondary education support. The Department then sat down, recognizing that they had a shortfall in their budget, and said, "We made some errors. Let us try to get better information from the bands who administer
the funding and let us put in a better budget for the following year."
So for the fiscal year 1988-89, the budget was submitted. Much better information was available. It was able to bring that down to 243 students, of which 0 were Bill C-31, that had to be deferred to the following semester. These deferrals occurred because the Department did not have all of the information. It still does not have all the information. So it is an estimate of the amount of funds that is going to be spent on post-secondary education for the following year. This year the Department submitted a budget figure of $130 million for post-secondary education under this program. Not one cent was cut back from that figure submitted by the Department. The Department was not asked to trim anything off the submitted figure. The $130 million was the figure that the Department, preparing their budget, estimated would cover every native or Indian student in Canada who wanted to participate in post-secondary education. That is the estimate, $130 million. I submit that we will know if that estimate is correct-in fact, it may be oversubmitted-but we will not know that until students enrol in September and again in January for the various semesters and until the fiscal year is over.
I therefore submit, Madam Speaker, to you and to my my friends in the House that it is incumbent on the Department to submit a budget item. It is incumbent on the Department to submit to Treasury Board an estimate of the funds it is going to spend. One can see from the pattern that they are trying very hard. We have a problem in that though. That problems exists in gathering the data from the bands.
Sixty-seven per cent of all the funds budgeted for post-secondary education are administered by Indian organizations. One hundred per cent of the 243 student deferrals in the 1988-89 fiscal year which ended March 31 occurred in Manitoba. The Manitoba Indian organizations administer almost 100 per cent of the post-secondary education budget in that region. There is a difficulty, and I am not blaming anyone. I want that clearly understood in this House. There is obviously a problem that exists in Manitoba in two-way communication that will bring any misbudgeting into line.
What has the Minister said in this House repeatedly? He has stated emphatically that the budget is in place, the objective is to cover every single Indian student who qualifies to partake in post-secondary education. That is the objective of the Minister. That is the objective of the Department. And that is the objective of every Member in this House of Commons.
April 24, 1989

They say there could be a shortfall. There well could be. But there could well be a surplus. We will not know until this fiscal year is over. So to talk about a cut-back or a cap is just not true. Any budget item submitted is the best possible guess using the best possible information at your disposal to say to Treasury Board, this is how much money you have to allocate. There would be a cut-back if it came back from Treasury Board and they said, no, you cannot have $130 million, you are going to have to cut it back to $110 million. But that did not happen. Not one cent was taken from the original submission to Treasury Board of $130 million. It was approved. So we will have to wait and see.
Let us go then to the bilateral process. The Minister has said to the students and the Indian organizations that he is prepared to sit down between now and September 1 in a bilateral process to discuss the policy and make any changes that would improve the delivery of the policy, the delivery of the system or indeed change the policy before September 1. He has asked in return that the students stop the hunger strike. That is a reasonable request, in my view.
What the Minister has really said goes back to the moratorium. The Minister in effect has agreed to a moratorium on implementing the policy between now and September 1, a moratorium on the policy he has in place now that has been submitted and been published. This is all in place. He will sit down with the students or student organizations between now and September 1. In effect, that is a moratorium. He has said that he is not going to throw out the policy and go back to what was in existence two years ago, because this policy recognizes the cost of living increases that some of the Members have been talking about and has actually increased all of the assistance, whether it is training allowance or whatever, to all of the students in every category.
I have seen one situation in which a student will have a reduction. I discussed this with the Minister. He said that the program could be flexible enough to accommodate any variances that might exist. The students now have an opportunity to sit down with the Minister to examine the Post-Secondary Education Assistance Program and to point out those areas which they believe are wrong or unworkable and have them changed. This can be done between today and September 1.
Supply
When I visited the students they asked why the Minister would publish this now and not sit down with them. They asked why this is done without their consultation, and there was an argument about whether or not there was consultation. Much of the policy itself was sent to the bands.
I have not been privy to the information about what the responses were, but the students who will be going to university in September had to know what the guidelines would be. All of them got an increase in their student assistance. I asked the Minister about the student whose assistance will actually drop and was told that he would be very flexible when sitting down with the students and would try to correct this problem.
My appeal to the students is that the time has come to sit down with the Minister. Now is the time to work on this policy because there is, in effect, a moratorium in place now. There is a moratorium until September 1.
The students say they would like a national student organization. I met with those students and found them to be articulate and bright. Some of them have real leadership qualities. If they want a national student organization, I suggest they go out and organize one. Of course they will have more strength with a national student organization.
When I was going to university I saw student organization develop in Canada, but it was developed by the students. The Government will not organize a national student organization; the onus is on the students to do it. "You have the intelligence. You are bright. You have the initiative. You have the leadership. Go ahead and do it".
I want some reason to come into this whole question. I would like my friends from the Official Opposition and the New Democratic Party to look at this as an issue about which no Member can claim sole moral integrity. We can all work together.
I believe our record has been exceptionally good in dealing with land claim settlements and many other issues we faced when we took office in 1984.1 have sat on the Standing Committee on Indian Affairs and Northern Development. I worked well with members of the Official Opposition and of the New Democratic Party. We were able to resolve some very serious issues, and often there was full agreement.

April 24, 1989
Supply
I travelled across the country on a special committee. Keith Penner, a former Member, did extremely well in the committee. There was a consensus to help native people.
Obviously, education is key to the development of native people. I have seen this development in many of the ridings, but education for many bands in many areas is still low. There is a lot of work to do. As has been stated over and over again, our Government is committed to supporting Indian students and post-secondary education.
There is no cap. We have not put a cap on post-secondary education for native students. Like every other Department, there is a budget which was arrived at with the best information possible. The budget figure was submitted on the basis that it would account for every student who qualified to go on to post-secondary education. It even allows for students who come from some of the communities with what they think are university entrance qualifications but are not. We have even accounted for community colleges so they can prepare themselves much better for a full university load.
I plead with all Members of the House to work together to try and resolve this issue. Our message to the students should be that it is time to stop the fast. It is time to come to the House of Commons, sit down with the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development (Mr. Cadieux), and resolve the situation as it should be resolved.
