speechtext:
Madam Speaker, after listening to the last speaker it would seem that he is prepared to ask the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development (Mr. Cadieux) to reconsider the capping. The Hon. Member said that there is no capping, so I would urge him to tell the Minister not to cap the post-secondary funding.
I am pleased to have the opportunity to participate in this important debate, and I would like to congratulate my colleague, the Hon. Member for Kenora-Rainy River (Mr. Nault), for sponsoring this significant motion on native post-secondary education. At the same time, as he has also acknowledged, it is unfortunate that this debate had to occur at all.
We would not be engaging the Government in this manner if we thought its policy was the right one. Fundamentally, what is at issue here is who decides what is best for aboriginal people, the Government or the aboriginal people themselves.
What is happening now in the case of post-secondary education is a classic conflict with respect to decision making between a Government that makes and imposes unilateral decisions and the aboriginal people who must live with those decisions.

April 24, 1989
Supply
The Government has characterized its new post-secondary program as being better and more generous than the program preceding it. It has said that it has consulted with Indian people. If that were the case, why have Indians across Canada risen up in protest? Why have several Indian students felt compelled to take the drastic step of a fast or a hunger strike to call attention to this situation?
The Government has tried to tell aboriginal people that it knows best what is good for them, and it has tried to convey that same message to the Canadian public. The aboriginal people of Canada are not buying that message, we on this side of the House are not buying it, and more and more Canadian people are not buying it.
The importance of obtaining higher education is a relatively new priority for aboriginal people. For the vast majority of us, until quite recently getting an education meant alienation from our people and our communities.
For years, young Indian and Inuit children were taken from their parents and sent away to residential schools where they received instruction in a foreign language about a foreign culture and where they were punished for speaking their own native language. When these children returned to their communities, they experienced great difficulties communicating with their parents and fitting back into the life-styles and ways of the community. They did not feel at ease in the non-aboriginal community. Is it any wonder that under these circumstances, most aboriginal people did not wish to pursue higher education? The costs in terms of loss of language, family, culture and identity were simply too high.
Fortunately the Government began to make greater efforts to reduce those human costs. It began building more schools in the communities where the people lived. It began to pay more attention to the fact that most Indian and Inuit were not even completing high school. More funding was provided to improve the large discrepancies in educational attainment between aboriginal and non-aboriginal people.
As educational services became more relevant to Indian and Inuit students, people began to realize that obtaining a higher education could be of benefit to themselves and to their communities. Education came to be looked at as the way out of the poverty and despair that continued to characterize their communities.
As more aboriginal students made it through the elementary and secondary levels and obtained the prerequisites for post-secondary studies, more decided to pursue higher learning. In 1960-61 only 60 Indian students were enrolled in university. In 1986-87 over 13,000 were enrolled in post-secondary institutions. In 1985-86, 933 Indian students graduated from universities and colleges. As more and more students entered the postsecondary system the budget increased. The Indian population has also increased. In 1961 there were approximately 192,000 Indians. In 1987 there were close to
416,000.
It is important for Hon. Members to realize that the aboriginal population is growing at a faster rate than the non-aboriginal population, and the Indian student population even more so in recent years due to the passage of Bill C-31. That Bill passed by the House in 1985 restored Indian status to thousands of Indian people who had lost it previously due to discriminatory provisions in the Indian Act. The Bill also made it possible for many others to obtain Indian status for the first time. Consequently, between 1985 and 1986 the Indian population increased by 7.7 per cent. Between 1986 and 1987 the population growth rate was 7.2 per cent.
Of great significance is the fact that the Indian population is very young. Sixty-four per cent are under the age of 25. Even the Department of Indian Affairs recognizes that the Indian leaders are coping with a baby boom which is creating major demands for education, employment, housing and other services.
The disparity between aboriginal and non-aboriginal economic conditions continues. Incomes remain substantially lower. The average income for Indians on reserves is 54 per cent of the average for the general population.
The recent report of the Canadian Human Rights Commission had a blunt message for the Government about the conditions of the aboriginal peoples. The report stated: "The situation faced by Canada's native peoples is in many ways a national tragedy. The grand promise of equality of opportunity that forms the central purpose of the Canadian Human Rights Act stands in stark contrast to the conditions in which many native people live''.
Despite the continuing social and economic discrepancies between aboriginal and non-aboriginal people, acknowledged most recently by the Canadian Human Rights Commissioner, the Government has decided to restrict the access of native people to the program which offers the best hope for the future.
April 24, 1989

The Government states that it has increased the post-secondary budget, and that Indian students can still get a post-secondary education under the new government guidelines. What the Government does not say is that the budget increase is below the increase in the number of students who are applying for funding. Therefore, a large number of Indian students will only be able to get their post-secondary education when it is convenient for the Government, and not when it is convenient for the students.
By placing a ceiling on the amount of funding available in a given fiscal year, by capping the program funding, the Government is restricting access. Students who apply for post-secondary assistance after the funds have been totally utilized will be turned down. That is a fact, and it has already happened. That is what the Indian students are protesting. Over the past two years hundreds of Indian students have been denied access to post-secondary institutions when they wanted to go, due to the lack of funding in the Department's program.
The Department of Indian Affairs refers to them as "deferred" students. These students meet the program criteria and have been accepted into the post-secondary institutions, but their applications for assistance have been refused because the Department has run out of money. They are told that they have to wait until money becomes available, either because some other student drops out, or because a new fiscal year brings a new budget. How can any student plan for the future under these circumstances?
With respect to the Government's claim to have consulted with Indian people about this policy, I would like to put this issue into proper perspective.
The Government's tinkering with this program began in late 1986 when it imposed a deadline for the receipt of students' applications. Many students were not even made aware of the deadline until it had passed.
Then in May, 1987, the previous Minister of Indian Affairs announced interim changes to the Post-secondary Education Assistance Program. He imposed a cap on the program budget at the time and instituted a system of priorities for student assistance. Student applications were placed into five categories and priorized by the Department of Indian Affairs. Those in category one
Supply
would receive assistance before those in category two, and so on. Students in category five would only receive funding if there was any money left over after all other categories had been funded.
Hon. Members should know that these changes were imposed on Indian people with no consultation whatsoever.
The Government knew that some students would not receive funding as a result of these interim changes to the program. In his letter of May 12 to the Indian Chiefs and Councils, the previous Minister of Indian Affairs, while announcing an increase in the budget, also stated: "Unlike the practice in previous years there will be no further increases later in this fiscal year. As a result, we may find ourselves faced with more eligible applicants than we can support".
The Minister also specified: "No appeal can be launched against a decision by the Department, a band council or tribal council who refuse assistance to a student on the basis that funds are no longer available regionally for student allowances".
Hon. Members should also know that the Minister was making these unilateral changes to the Post-secondary Education Assistance Program without waiting for the results of a major study on education being conducted by the Assembly of First Nations. Funding for the study was promised by the previous Liberal Government, and this commitment was upheld by the new Government's Minister of Indian Affairs, the former Member for Rosedale.
In his announcement of May, 1987, the Minister also stated that further modifications to the program were necessary. Naturally, Indian people expected that their study, when completed, would figure prominently in future directions for the program. Unfortunately, according to the Assembly of First Nations, this is not the case. The new program guidelines do not have the support or approval of the Indian people.
The Government must change the way it deals with aboriginal people and their concerns. What it calls consultation is very much one way, the Government's way. If Indian people had truly participated in decisionmaking on this issue, we would not be debating this issue today.

April 24, 1989
Supply
There has been much discussion about figures and data over the past few days. In his speech last Friday the Minister referred to the need for better data in order to forecast demand and costs better. The Minister would be well advised not to rely too much on his departmental officials to obtain that data. It will probably be inaccurate, as it has usually been.
As an example, I refer to his Department's forecasting of the number of Indians who would be eligible for Indian status as a result of the passage of Bill C-31. Those forecasts were grossly inadequate. His predecessor admitted that in this Chamber in response to a question posed by the former opposition critic for Indian Affairs and Northern Development, the former Member for Cochrane-Superior. This colossal miscalculation was noted in the Fifth Report of the Standing Committee on Aboriginal Affairs and Northern Development which was submitted to the House last August.
The report noted that although the Department had originally estimated 65,000 applicants, it had been obliged, on the basis of applications pouring in, to revise that number upwards to 118,000.
When that Bill was in the House and in committee, Indian people told the Government and the Minister of the day that the Department's figures were far too low. The Government did not listen. It is no wonder aboriginal people are skeptical about the Department's ability to plan and budget properly.

Madam Speaker, I welcome this opportunity to take part in this debate, because I have several Indian families in my riding, and especially because of the fact that for twelve years, when I was an insurance broker and businessman, I did business with the Indians on the Kahnawake reserve, and I have always had a keen interest their circumstances, both present and future.
Madam Speaker, a number of serious allegations have been made in recent weeks about the Government's commitment to providing funding for the post-secondary education of Indians and Inuit. Today, Madam Speaker, I would like to take this opportunity to set the record straight and give the House the assurance that we will continue to promote the interests of Canada's Indians and Inuit through education.
Here in Ottawa, Madam Speaker, a small group of Indian students have put their physical well-being at risk by starting a hunger strike to protest against the Post-Secondary Education Assistance Program announced last month.
These students are trying to obtain a moratorium on this policy. Such a moratorium is unnecessary, regressive and might be harmful to the interests of the majority of the students.
Madam Speaker, I am troubled by this gesture, and I find it hard to understand what they are trying to do. The new policy is clearly an improvement, if we compare it with the previous program known as the E-12 guidelines.
When the Post-Secondary Assistance Program was announced, the Government indicated that it would always be willing to consider recommendations from the Indian community.
Madam Speaker, the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development also offered to work directly with the Assembly of First Nations, other Indian leaders and student representatives on a joint policy research and development program.
Under this proposal, all aspects of the program would be examined. Meanwhile, the new Post-Secondary Education Assistance Program would be available to students for the academic year 1989-90.
Madam Speaker, Hon. Members are aware that the Post-Secondary Education Assistance Program is one of the most successful programs ever undertaken by this Department.
Under the E-12 guidelines, the number of post-secondary students rose from 3,500 when the program was introduced in 1977-78 to about 15,000 in 1988-89. During the same period, the program's budget rose from $9 million to nearly $130 million.
Madam Speaker, we realize that even the most successful programs need updating and revising from time to time to meet changing of needs and emerging trends.
Madam Speaker, in this case, there was a need to increase the number of graduates, in other words, to ensure that larger numbers of Indian students finish their college or university education. And that, Madam Speaker, bearing in mind that the program's budget has to reflect today's economic reality.
A year ago, this Government announced that a consultation process would be initiated to make changes in the E-12 guidelines.
As part of this process, a draft policy was sent to all regions of the country, and meetings were held with Indian groups.
Madam Speaker, we were clearly committed to formulating a policy that met Indian and Inuit needs and aspirations.
Between July and December last year, representatives of Indian Affairs and Northern Development consulted with about 500 bands, tribal councils and students' groups.
April 24, 1989

These groups expressed their concerns and their recommendations were given serious thought. Following these consultations, the draft proposal which had been distributed in July 1988 was thoroughly revised.
Hon. Members who are familiar with the national study of the Assembly of First Nations on Indian education may have noticed that most of the study's recommendations concerning post-secondary education have been incorporated in the new policy. For instance, the Post-Secondary Education Assistance Program provides incentives and scholarships for students who want to take a course of study that would contribute directly to achieving Indian self-government and economic self-reliance.
Under the new policy, Madam Speaker, administering organizations have an even greater opportunity to participate directly in the post-secondary education process. The policy also establishes uniform rates of assistance which apply across the country, instead of the regional variations contained in the E-12 guidelines. Madam Speaker, the new policy also provides direct support to a number of Indian post-secondary institutions.
The new policy is a definite improvement over the E-12 guidelines in practically all respects. Tuition fees are now covered, regardless of time spent in post-secondary education. Allowances for living expenses are generally higher. These allowances range from $200 up to $1,355 per month for a married student with a spouse and three other dependants. Fifty dollars per month is provided for each additional dependant.
Madam Speaker, the new policy also provides for higher allowances for students living in areas where rental costs are highest.
Madam Speaker, these increased allowances are the direct result of the consultation process that I already mentioned. Moreover, the limits on student aid have been restructured. A student can now receive assistance for a college program, an undergraduate program and a program leading to a graduate diploma or a professional degree.
Students can also receive assistance for studies leading to a second bachelor's degree when a first bachelor's degree is a prerequisite. The new policy also presents an innovative system of incentive awards. The E-12 guidelines did not provide this kind of incentive. Indian and Inuit postgraduate students will receive a scholarship of
Supply
up to $1,500. In addition, they will receive a special incentive award of up to $3,500 a year that will be given to students in programs that foster Indian self-government and economic self-reliance.
The new policy, Madam Speaker, also provides for scholarships to recognize academic success that will be awarded to students who maintain a B average or higher in their college or undergraduate program.
Madam Speaker, it is ironic that we are criticized for having set specific fields of study for the special incentive awards. The Assembly of First Nations recommended that we take such an approach. The changes to the program will ensure greater fairness and uniformity in administering this program. They will make it possible to put greater emphasis on academic success and obtaining a diploma. They will also enable Indian organizations to exercise greater control and provide better support for the objectives of Indian self-government and economic development.
Madam Speaker, this program is essential for Indians to take charge of their future. It is a good program. It is a generous program. In reality, it is the best in the world. A moratorium at this time would only benefit a limited number of students; a much larger number would suffer. We must therefore go ahead with this program and we intend to do so. I urge the Minister to do so.

subtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 81-POST-SECONDARY EDUCATION FUNDING-NATIVE PEOPLES
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I want to first of all congratulate my colleague, the Hon. Member for Kenora-Rainy River (Mr. Nault), for putting forward this exceptionally important motion which has occupied the attention of the House during the past two days. At the same time I would like to congratulate the Hon. Member for Nunat-siaq (Mr. Anawak), our colleague in the Senate, Len Marchand, for his efforts in the last few days to help resolve what has become a very sad situation. May I also pay particular tribute to my colleague, the Hon. Member for Western Arctic (Ms. Blondin), who is our Liberal critic on aboriginal affairs. She has lately put in very long nights attempting in a reasonable way to make our Government see the unreasonableness of its policies. The Hon. Member for Western Arctic is doing the job with our native people that the Minister should be doing.
I want to congratulate these Hon. Members, but I do so with a good deal of sorrow because it is unbelievably regrettable that in a country as rich and generous as Canada, we have a Government which refuses to provide basic rights to our native peoples.
What is happening in this country today is quite straightforward. The Conservative Government since the election has dropped any facade of moderation. It has stripped away the election rhetoric. It has become a right-wing bully-boy. The velvet glove of campaign promises has been replaced with the brass knuckles of tough-guy politics.
The Government is engaged in a three-part strategy. First, dishonour those election commitments where they cost too much; thereby, of course, bringing discredit upon the whole profession of politics in this country. Secondly, to act vindictively toward any people, any group of people or any province that may disagree with the Government. The recent outburst from the Florida Panhandle of the Minister of Trade in respect to the election of Clyde Wells as the new Premier of Newfoundland is typical. Thirdly, make the most disadvantaged, the most defenceless, the most impoverished,

April 24, 1989
Supply
those without clout, make those people in our country pay first for four and a half years of Conservative economic mismanagement.
I suppose you might say that that is a harsh indictment. But it is one that the Government has brought upon itself. Listen to what the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) used to say. He told the First Ministers' Conference in April, 1985, and I use his words, "As a Canadian and as a Prime Minister, I fully recognize and agree with the emphasis the aboriginal peoples place on having their special rights. Improvements to the economic and social circumstances of aboriginal peoples must be pursued at the same time as changes to our Constitution. Action is required on both fronts."
The Prime Minister also said, and I quote him once again, "Policies regarding aboriginal people will be made after open public consultation, especially at the grass roots level". That was what the Prime Minister used to say up to and during the election campaign. How can he possibly reconcile those words with the policy of capping funding for native post-secondary education? I have heard the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development (Mr. Cadieux) say in this House that he has consulted over 500 native groups across the country. What he does not say and what we have learned is that not one of those 500 groups agree with this particular policy.
So there we have it, part one of the current Tory strategy: break your word at every opportunity. You can get away with it. Then we move to part two of his strategy: the tough guy vindictive attitude.

A group of native students is on a hunger strike to protest a policy that is contrary to the Prime Minister's own commitments. These students are on a hunger strike to draw attention to the urgent need for funds for post-secondary education. What is the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development (Mr. Cadieux) doing? Will he sit down with these students to discuss their legitimate concerns? Does he remember that he too was once a student and that he was a student protester? No! He treats them as though they were guilty of a criminal offence. He is inflexible. He tells them to go back to school. He makes them understand that he, the Minister in the federal Cabinet, is the one who matters and that the students do not have the right to speak on behalf of the native people of the country. He makes them a promise. He tells them that if they end
their hunger strike, he is ready to negotiate with them in good faith. Some students take him at his word. They suspend their strike. They meet the Minister and he answers them, in effect: What you are doing is useless. I do not intend to change my policy.
These young men and women, already on the 32nd day of their hunger strike, are endangering their health. The Minister is deaf to all pleas and absolutely refuses to be moved.
The Government and the Minister are so afraid of being weak that they forget that it shows greater strength of character to be open to forgiveness and pity.

So we come to the third part of the Tory strategy: make the weak and the poor, the dispossessed and the disadvantaged pay for the Government's mismanagement. Make the most disadvantaged people in the country pay for deficit reduction. As the Commissioner for Human Rights said in his last annual report-these are Mr. Yalden's words-"An Indian youngster in Canada has a better chance of being sent to prison than completing university". What an indictment. In the face of that indictment, what does this Government do? They cap appropriation for native post-secondary education and they deny hundreds of native Canadians the opportunity to go to university.
Let us have a few facts on the floor of the House, Madam Speaker. Today, more than half of Canada's native population is under 20 years of age. Any government that wanted to call itself enlightened would see that native post-secondary education is a tremendous opportunity to end the cycle of poverty among our aboriginal people. It is bitter irony that the results and achievements and participation of Indian students under the program are the very reasons the Government gives for denying other Indian students access to the program.
This program has been a success story. The Minister likes to boast about it. He tells the House how much more money has been spent on it. Why? It is because the native young people of this country finally recognize that the one way out is education. They have flocked to this program because they know they can have a better life than their ancestors have had since the white man came to this continent. That is what they are concerned about. It has been the success of the program that has prompted the Government to cap it.
April 24, 1989

The income level of native Canadians is only 50 per cent of the national average. The unemployment rate among native Canadians averages 55 per cent. We know that it is well over 90 per cent on some reserves.
What does the Government do? It reduces levels of assistance to individual students, making it difficult or impossible for many to complete their education.
I want to bring some more alarming statistics to Your Honour's attention. Only 20 per cent of native Canadians have finished high school, compared to 75 per cent of all Canadians. Nearly 40 per cent of native Canadians have less than Grade 8 education. Violent deaths among aboriginal peoples are three times the national average. Infant mortality is 60 per cent higher than the national average. Hospital admissions are two and one-half times the national average. The life expectancy of native peoples is 10 years less than the national average.
What does the Government do? It does a cost control exercise on the one program that was providing native people with the initiative, the gumption, the hope, the commitment to broaden their aspect of life and become more fully Canadian and able to participate with what the country has to offer. It is one program that was really working, because 90 per cent of all Indian young people who have achieved post-secondary education are employed.

The Minister, who is entering upon this portfolio, should be looking for ways to enhance his credibility with his constituents, the native people who he represents on the floor of the House of Commons.

This is a program of native post-secondary education which is working and produces a healthy, trained group of young Canadians from the native community. It is a program from which 90 per cent of them are now gainfully, usefully employed.
Given a choice between that and the foolish alternative of limiting native post-secondary education, what would that do? It leads to more unemployment. It leads to more violence. It leads to more drug abuse. It leads to far higher cost in social assistance. The Government has chosen the wrong course of action, a disastrous course of action.

Nevertheless, it cannot be said that the program is not working. In 20 years, the proportion of native students attending university has increased from 1 to 12 per cent. Of course, this is still less than the national average, but the progress is encouraging. We can be optimistic, the potential is there and solutions are in sight.
The Government cannot say either that it did not know that passage of Bill C-31 would result in increased demand for post-secondary education for native people.

The Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) tries to take credit on the one hand for Bill C-31, which has encouraged approximately 110,000 native people to seek reinstatement under the Indian Act.
On the other he is saying, now that we have this increase in population, that we cannot afford the primary program which allows the next generation to succeed. That lack of logic does not persuade me and should not persuade the Minister. That is why the Human Rights Commissioner called the treatment of our native peoples a national tragedy.
Despite this two-day debate, the Government seems hell-bent on perpetuating that national tragedy. Are the requests by the Assembly of First Nations so unreasonable? Is it so unreasonable to request a moratorium on the new policy until next April 1? Is it so unreasonable to remove a cap on post-secondary education all together? The Conservatives' own Member, the Hon. Member for Wetaskiwin (Mr. Littlechild), did not think so when he marched against the Government's policy on March 22.1 give him credit for guts.

April 24, 1989
Supply
I say to the Minister that if the Government will not listen to the students, if it will not listen to the leaders of the native people, the Assembly of First Nations, if it will not listen to us here in the Opposition, surely the Minister might listen to his own Member of Parliament who knew what he was doing and is close to his people.
I am simply saying to the Minister that of all the promises to break-and there will be a good many of them broken here Thursday afternoon when the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) stands up-do not break the ones given to our aboriginal peoples. Of all the groups in the country with whom the Government wants to get tough, do not get tough with young people who are pressing for justice. Of all the programs that are up for review, do not cap the one program which is really working, which is truly working in bringing an end to over 200 years of injustice and discrimination, poverty and despair among our native people.
There is still an opportunity for the Government to bring some honour to itself in this sad affair. There is still an opportunity for the Minister to regain credibility with the constituents he should be representing in the House. I urge the Minister and the Government to seize that opportunity.
Far more important than the Government's credibility, than the Minister's sense of esteem with the native people, far more important, there is still an opportunity for the Government to provide more hope for our native people. I urge the Government to provide that hope.
This is as human an issue as we have had for a long time in the House of Commons. This is why our Members are so incensed by it, and why members of the New Democratic Party are concerned. This is why we asked for a two-day debate to use the precious time given to us as Opposition in the House of Commons, because nothing is more important to us than the fiduciary relationship we have-

-our position of trust, especially towards the next generation, which is already disadvantaged.

I want the Minister to take this all very seriously because nothing has gripped our sense of purpose more than this debate and this particular subject.

speechtext: Hear, hear!

subtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 81-POST-SECONDARY EDUCATION FUNDING-NATIVE PEOPLES
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I listened with interest to the right hon. gentleman's discussion of the issue. My question for him is one to which I have not been able to get an answer from his colleagues.
I am sure the right hon. gentleman is aware of the fact that one of the three demands of the students is recognition of post-secondary education as a treaty right. Will the Right Hon. Member answer the House once and for all on whether or not his Party supports the idea that has been dodged so artfully by his colleagues over the last few days? Does he support post-secondary education as a treaty right?

subtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 81-POST-SECONDARY EDUCATION FUNDING-NATIVE PEOPLES
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I will answer the Hon. Member directly. However, I want to preamble what I have to say by suggesting that whether or not this is a treaty right it is a human right for every young person in this country to have a right to education.
Her Government has never recognized the inherent constitutional rights of our native peoples, the rights that preceded the arrival of the British Crown on the northern half of this continent.
There are those bands who sincerely believe that in the way their treaties were drafted, education is among those treaty rights. Coming back to Ottawa the other day, I was on the airplane with the Hon. Ray Hnatyshyn and we argued this particular issue.
Many of the bands feel that within their particular treaties, education is among those rights guaranteed by the British Crown. We would have to examine the whole panoply of treaties. We have consistently felt, however, that fundamental to the rights of any young person is the right to education, particularly for Indian people living on the reserves. It is the only way to break out of the cycle of poverty and despair. The Hon. Member raises her eyebrows but I am saying that the only way out is education.
The program started 20 years ago and it is working. The reason the Minister has to cap it is that it is working. There is not a fraud here. There is not a crime here. There is not a group deceit here. There is a desperate attempt on the part of a whole generation of young Indian and native peoples to join us within the full rights of Canadians. That is what this is about.
April 24, 1989

Frankly, I would be prepared, if I were given the brief, to argue the treaty rights as including education. To be absolutely frank to the Hon. Member at this stage, we must go back and examine the language of every one of those treaties.

speakeroldname: Mrs. Dorothy Dobbie (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
subtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 81-POST-SECONDARY EDUCATION FUNDING-NATIVE PEOPLES
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, it gives me a great deal of pleasure to rise today to speak on this issue. I have listened very carefully over the last few days and have heard many, many comments. I have heard a lot of misinformation and much of the misinformation came this afternoon, shockingly enough, from my right hon. colleague across the way.
I would like to set the record straight on a couple of things. Consultation did take place with over 500 groups. The Right Hon. Member is mistaken when he suggests that not one of those groups supported the new policy. That simply is not so.
I would also like to remind the Right Hon. Member that the Minister has met with the students who stopped their strike, and he listened very carefully to what was being said. He did this in preparation for further dialogue with the students. If we do not build that kind of relationship in which there can be honest and open dialogue, we will not resolve the outstanding questions, and there surely will be outstanding questions. The Minister has established a relationship with the native community that will be very productive for us in the future.
We have all listened over the last few days to my colleagues who have been discussing the Indian Post-Secondary Student Assistance Program with a great deal of vigour. As they have pointed out, in many cases it is one of the most successful programs the Department of Indian Affairs or this Government has ever undertaken. It was originally designed to encourage registered Indians and Inuit to get a post-secondary education to help them achieve economic self-sufficiency.
Under the new program the objective is to encourage graduation, to get them out of school and into the jobs in order to pursue those 90 per cent of opportunities we just heard about. However, they must do so with the qualifications and skills that are necessary to get those jobs in the first place. Of course, the ultimate goal is
Supply
Indian self-government and economic self-reliance, a worthy goal that I am sure my right hon. friend will support.
In fact, the program is an excellent one. It is carefully tailored to meet the needs of Indian students. To help dispel the confusion over the program, confusion that has been again created today, I would like to go over some of the highlights of it because they bear repeating.
First, the budget for the post-secondary education program has increased significantly in recent years. There has been a steady increase in funding which has grown from $4.2 million in 1975-76 to $130 million this year. In addition, specific additional funding has been provided to meet the needs of students who have regained Indian status under Bill C-31. In fact, during the past two years alone, the budget has increased by 10 per cent in each of those years to meet the needs of additional students.
Each year carefully compiled estimates are made of the number of students expected to apply for entry into the program in the coming year, and the appropriate funds are budgeted according to those estimates. That is a reasonable approach. Under the new policy students will be eligible to receive funding while they attend such things as upgrading classes. They will be eligible to receive funding to go to community colleges or to obtain undergraduate degrees. Should they wish to obtain advanced or professional degrees, there will be funding for that as well.
Student allowances will be provided for the official length of the program-three years for a three-year program, four years for a four-year program and so on. In addition, a year at each level may be provided when required for a student to complete a degree or diploma program.
Under the old E-12 guidelines tuition assistance had specific student month limits which governed tuition allowances and registration fees for individual designated periods, and the maximum limit of possible assistance was 96 student months. Under the new program there are no time limits to tuition assistance. There are time limits governing living allowances, but these limits continue to provide support for a student from the first year right through to the doctorate level.

April 24, 1989
Supply
Students are also eligible to receive support for university preparation if it is required. We want students to plan their programs with an eye to completing their studies to a successful conclusion that will allow them to play a vital and active role in Canadian life. The program is designed to achieve this.
The new guidelines also provide a national standard rate structure for living allowances which replaces what went before, a confusing and wide range of regionally determined rates. The new program will guarantee equal treatment for students across Canada. Just in case there is a problem, the new standard rate generally represents an increase over average rates provided under the old policy.
For example, a single student living away from home now gets an average of $675 per month compared to $667 last year. In addition certain students, with dependants, studying in very high rental areas will be eligible for an increased monthly allowance to cover additional housing needs.
My colleagues have previously pointed out that grants for single students are equivalent to a full-time job paying $4.96 per hour. The grants paid to a single parent student with three dependants are equivalent to a full-time job paying $12.14 per hour, but I think these points bear repeating. That is not all. There are also annual scholarships of up to $3,500 for those who successfully undertake studies in areas which will aid Indian self-government and economic development. Students who follow programs in commerce, business and public administration, economics, science, mathematics, computer sciences, forestry and engineering will have an additional incentive to pursue these studies with great vigour.
Our program is gearing up for excellence, and we are determined that native people will be equipped to manage their own affairs, equipped with the appropriate education. In pursuit of this goal, students who work hard and do well are also eligible for annual scholarships of $1,000 based on academic achievement. These awards are available to up to 5 per cent of the student enrolment in each category. This is a significant improvement over the old policy which did not provide for this kind of support and encouragement.
Perhaps one of the most important aspects of this policy is the fact that it can be administered by Indian leaders themselves, the people who are in a position to
see that the program meets the real needs of the students it is designed for. This kind of self-supervision can only enhance, in my opinion, the effectiveness of the program and contribute to the dignity of those who are enrolled in it. I think that is extremely important.
As for the amount of funding, we have heard a great deal about that in the last couple of days. We have heard much negative comment from our hon. colleagues opposite. I can only report that this student assistance program is one of the most generous of its kind in the world.
I pointed out earlier today that there are 15,000 students in the United States who shared a total funding of $32.9 million last year. That compares to Canada's
15,000	students, the same number of students, who will share $130 million in funding this year. Canadian Indian students receive almost four times the support of their American counterparts. Clearly that demonstrates the new policy is a reasonable one and a responsible one which represents a great improvement over the previous guidelines.
The Government is not only listening to the concerns of the Indian and Inuit people. It is also responding to those concerns. The Minister has repeatedly stated that he is totally open to all suggestions for improvement to the program. I do not know how he can make it any clearer. He has demonstrated his willingness to make adjustments where shown to be desirable and sensible.
The Government has played a leadership role in improving opportunities for access of Indian and Inuit students to post-secondary education. It is no accident that enrolment has risen from fewer than 3,500 in the late 1970s to more than 15,000 today. We heard the Hon. Member congratulate us on the success of the program that brought the numbers to 15,000.
Our policies have been instrumental in opening forever the educational doors that were closed to our native communities in the past, including the period of time when Members opposite were in a position of power and in a position to make decisions that would have had a long lasting beneficial effect on the native peoples of the country and perhaps would have had them advance far beyond where they are now. However, we are starting with something, and I think we are making tremendous progress.
April 24, 1989

In the last few days we have heard a great deal of lip-service in the House, but we are doing more than simply paying lip-service to the importance of post-secondary education in the economic, social and political development of Indian and Inuit communities.
We have developed policies and have provided funding to ensure that there will be more Indian doctors, nurses, engineers, commerce graduates, lawyers, teachers, and other professionals. The new policy builds on previous successes and significantly enhances the opportunity for Indian students successfully to complete courses of study which will allow them to engage in useful and rewarding occupations that will put them in the mainstream of Canadian life. That is the point of this program.
Indian students must have access to post-secondary education today if they are to take advantage of tomorrow's employment opportunities. We all agree with that. We all feel strongly that if they are to be able to develop and operate their own businesses and institutions of self-government and contribute to a better quality of life in their communities, as well as play an active role in Canadian society, the educational system must be relevant and must produce graduates.
The Indian and Inuit people have a great deal to offer and much to contribute to Canada. Their affinity with the land and their understanding of the natural order of things have much to teach us, and we must be prepared to listen. When listening we must open our hearts and our ears in order to get a better understanding and thereby benefit from this experience. The Government and the Minister realize this. I believe the Minister is wise in his knowledge that productive dialogue can only take place in an atmosphere free from coercion.
In conclusion, it is important to commend the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development (Mr. Ca-dieux) for his dedication and leadership in introducing this policy for post-secondary student assistance. The program is one of the finest and most successful that Canada has ever developed. If Hon. Members opposite were to search their hearts and be honest, I believe they would admit that it is a generous, fair and reasonable program. The Minister is also to be congratulated for his commitment to Indian and Inuit people in general, and for his leadership and his commitment to post-secondary education.
Supply
The negative reaction that we have seen and heard in the media is most unfortunate, and it is most unfortunate that it is based on inaccurate information and inaccurate perceptions. There is still a perception that the draft policy which was used as a basis for the consultations which were carried out was used as a basis for the final policy. I would like to make it veiy clear and set the record straight that the final policy has been revised and improved as a result of that consultation process.
The Minister has repeatedly stated his willingness to make more changes and further improvements should they be needed. He is willing and eager to sit down in a calm and rational fashion to discuss additional changes and improvements. The consultations are not over. They are ongoing and continuing. The policy has changed and it will continue to change with the times.
In 1977-78 it cost $9 million to send 3,500 Indian students to university or college. That has been improved and 15,000 are covered under a budget of $130 million. The program will be continually improved as the need arises. It must be continually reviewed to address appropriately the changing needs and the aspirations of Indian youth. It is a reasonable and a responsible program that offers a better way of life, a life of independence and dignity for the coming generation of native people. I believe that the Minister and the program deserve the full support of the House.

subtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 81-POST-SECONDARY EDUCATION FUNDING-NATIVE PEOPLES
speechtext:
First, I listened with a great deal of interest to the very fine speech given by our own colleague, the Hon. Member for Nunatsiaq (Mr. Ana-wak). I only wish that the Hon. Member who just completed her remarks had listened a little more closely.
Second, I wish that the Hon. Member had sat in on the hearings or read the transcripts of the hearings held by the Standing Committee on Indian Affairs. I was a member of that committee when it changed the Indian Act to recognize and acknowledge women in the Indian society.
I certainly recall the two meetings of the First Ministers' Conferences in which I was in attendance. I was also part of the committee that looked at employment equity and, sad to say, recognized the inadequacies of that Bill, as well as the Indian Act.
We now recognize something that the Member does not seem to have thought about, the fact that we have had a very large increase in a young population. We have a vibrant source of new employers and new employees in Canada, and the Hon. Member does not care to ac-

April 24, 1989
Supply
knowledge the aboriginal people's potential contribution to the growth and development of this land, which is their land. This is our land; this is their land. They are part and parcel of that land.
If the theory the Hon. Member was propounding were applied to the Unemployment Insurance Act, we would only pay off the first half or quarter who applied. If the theory were applied to those who are now arriving at age 65, perhaps old age security would not be paid after the month of March or April because the funds would have run out.
Is that the way the Hon. Member is suggesting, first come first served? Is there to be a cap because there are too many bright, young, competent people who have evolved through a system which has only been in operation a bare 20 years?
It is effective, but it is being capped because it costs too much money. If the cap were removed and all the brave young students were served-and I do not particularly agree with the procedure used-it would cost the equivalent of one five-thousandth of the national debt. If the moratorium were taken off, it would cost one-fiftieth of 1 per cent of the national debt.
Would the Hon. Member tell me why those young people, the future of the country, are being attacked for that type of extra money which is equal to one-half the money the Government spent on advertising in the past year? What is the Hon. Member's point, and what is her beef?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
subtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 81-POST-SECONDARY EDUCATION FUNDING-NATIVE PEOPLES
speechtext: Madam Speaker, obviously the Hon. Member is the one who doesn't listen or she would not have made some of the comments that she did.

subtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 81-POST-SECONDARY EDUCATION FUNDING-NATIVE PEOPLES
speechtext: Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
subtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 81-POST-SECONDARY EDUCATION FUNDING-NATIVE PEOPLES
speechtext:
All students who wish to apply for post-secondary education in Canada will be accommodated. There is no question that there will be dollars to pay for those students to go to school. If the estimates are not accurate-and we have said from the very beginning that there is a possibility that the estimates may be lacking because we do not have the kind of tight data we need-some applicants may have to wait a year to get into the program. But I wish the Hon. Member would stop trying to twist the facts and pay attention to us when we say that all students will eventually be
accommodated, that no students are being turned away or deprived of a post-secondary education.
We are not talking about theory here. The Hon. Member mentioned a theory. I think we all agree, and I listened very carefully to her remarks, that education is a fundamental need, a fundamental right of all human beings. There is no question about that. Indian youth and adult Indian students are as entitled to post-secondary education of a high quality as anyone else in this country. If we can do anything at all to make it easier for them to access that, we will. As I have said, and as the Minister has said repeatedly, there is plenty of opportunity to make adjustments where it is required. If a student feels that he has in some way slipped through the cracks, the Minister's door is open. He will listen and he will try to accommodate. Surely there is not much more that this Government could do to accommodate the needs of Indian and Inuit students in this country.

subtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 81-POST-SECONDARY EDUCATION FUNDING-NATIVE PEOPLES
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I might ask one question that has been asked a number of times but to which we still have not had an answer. If I heard correctly, the Hon. Parliamentary Secretary said that under this program some students will have to wait a year to go to a post-secondary institution. If that is what she said, might she say it again so we can all hear it clearly?
There is another question that has been asked three or four times. Supposing under the present scheme the number of students who apply are in excess of the number of dollars available for post-secondary education. In other words, there is not enough money in the present $130 million to enable whatever number of students who apply to go to a post-secondary education institution. Will the Government automatically increase the budget to make available sufficient funds for students to gain access to post-secondary education? Or will the Government prevent some students from gaining entry to post-secondary education institutions through lack of funding? Can we not have a simple answer to a simple question? Will there be some students left without adequate funding to go to post-secondary education institutions if the $130 million does not cover those who apply? If there are a few extra students, will they get funding? It is a very simple question and it has been asked about eight times, yet we still do not have an answer.
April 24, 1989

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
subtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 81-POST-SECONDARY EDUCATION FUNDING-NATIVE PEOPLES
speechtext:
The answer has been given before. Madam Speaker. The Minister has given the answer repeatedly, and the answer is simple. First, some students may have to wait up to a year. Will there be money to take care of their needs when the appropriate time comes after that period when the next budget is set? The Minister has stated that he will find the funds to cover the needs of the students. He will go to Treasury Board and ask that the budget be set at a higher rate for the subsequent year.
I think Hon. Members opposite have to agree that it is only good, sound, sensible management that sets a budget for any program. We do not write blank cheques for anything we do in this country. If we do, we end up in the kind of trouble that we are in right now, so far in debt that we are becoming a laughing stock to the rest of the world. This Government is trying to run a fair, reasonable and generous policy under guidelines that will allow for planning and for appropriate budget-setting for the future. There is nothing unreasonable and nothing difficult about that.

subtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 81-POST-SECONDARY EDUCATION FUNDING-NATIVE PEOPLES
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, it is my pleasure to be the final speaker on this very important two days of debate in this House. I do so as the Member of Parliament for some of those people who were on a hunger strike, for some of those who are currently on a hunger strike, and for approximately 800 students at Lakehead University and Confederation College in Thunder Bay, 800 individuals who have chosen to pursue a new future for themselves and for their communities. They see this policy, this change brought in by the Conservative Government to the E-12 guidelines, as limiting the abilities of their brothers and sisters, both literally and in blood, from getting the same kind of access they are now enjoying.
There is nothing that provides greater pleasure than going to the graduation ceremonies at Lakehead University each spring and seeing, year after year, more and more native students graduating. They are graduating from special native study programs, aiming to return to their reserves to work in concert with their peers, their elders and their children. As well, they are aiming to get into the so-called mainstream by applying for jobs
Supply
outside the reserves to provide services to native and non-native alike. As Bob Rosehart, the President of Lakehead University is quoted as saying in Saturday's Star. "These people provide the very positive role models that the communities themselves have been seeking, to say, yes, we can do it. It is not only possible for us to go to Thunder Bay and get an education at the post-secondary level and to come back with a diploma or a degree, but we can bring back with us the knowledge that will assist our communities, be they reserve-based communities or non-reserve communities, in improving our ability to be self-sustainable as a society". That is why it is important that we maximize this investment by the Canadian taxpayers in the educational system.
Just before I spoke there was an exchange between one of my colleagues and the Parliamentary Secretary, who clearly said there would be up to a one year delay for those people who wish to take post-secondary education under this program, but because of a funding cap they would be unable to do so. Who will be the ones delayed? Will they be the high school graduates who come from far northern or remote communities? Will they be told they will have to wait for another year? We know, and there are those who have more expertise in this than I, that the moment you break the educational pattern, the chances of going back to school are virtually nil, particularly for females.
Will it be the adult students who, after years of welfare perhaps, or employment that is not conducive to their community or because we, as a society, have destroyed their natural resources, be they fish, animal, forests or what have you, all of a sudden finally get it all together and say, yes, I have the motivation to go back to school and learn something I was unable to do as a child? More than likely, some did not even complete high school, if they ever went to high school. Are we now to say they will have to wait one more year because we do not have enough dollars and cents. We do not have that extra $9,000 to take them from their remote community to a Thunder Bay or to a Saskatoon or some other city with a university or community college? After those individuals have developed their own motivation, because they know the resources are there, are we going to say no? And does that really mean that we are saying no forever because they will ask, why bother?

April 24, 1989
Supply
Every time we throw another road block in the paths of native Canadians we are doing them a disservice. We should be bending over backwards to give native Canadians full access to our post-secondary education. Not just for a B.A. With all due respect for those who have their B.A., what can you do with a B.A.? You do not even need a B.A. to run for Parliament. You can actually be a high school dropout and get here as well. But the important thing is that they have to have the ability to go on to get into the professions. Doctors, lawyers, accountants, pharmacists and nurses, the whole gamut are important for these communities to have the skills practised by people who are their own, so that they understand the nuances, understand the needs. That is why this is so important.
A lot has been said about the Minister's desire or willingness to keep talking between now and September, and that if the Minister can be convinced that there is a need to change it, he will change it. But the reality is that those individuals who are planning to go to first-year university or first-year community college next year must plan that now.
Our kids are waiting for decisions from the universities as to whether they are accepted. Native kids are too. They need to know that the dollars and cents are in place so that they can make that commitment, so that when school starts on September 4 or 5, they will be there. They need to know about accommodation. They cannot find accommodation the week before university starts. They need to line that up months ahead. If they are coming from one of those small isolated reserves in northern Canada, in northern parts of the provinces, or in an area that is distant from the educational centre, and they are moving not just themselves but are moving children and spouses, they need the time to properly plan and make arrangements in order to have appropriate accommodations for their needs.
That is why we have said put it on hold for now, put a moratorium in place, at least on the negative aspects of the changes, so that the First Nations for the students can work with the Minister and the Department to develop appropriate guidelines that will allow an implementation in September of 1990 so that we do not disenfranchise or delay anybody and that those natives who wish to go to secondary education can do so.
If there is some abuse, as the Minister has suggested in his letters to the Chiefs, then let us deal with that. George Erasmus indicated quite clearly in the Star on Saturday that they are prepared as a community to work out the rules so that nobody gets a free ride per se. The ministry quite clearly does not have any proof of anybody taking advantage of the program, for example going for eight years and not getting any final diploma or degree, but if those things do exist, let the First Nations work out the rules with the ministry. The important thing is that we do put a moratorium in place, that we give the native people a chance to work it out with the Minister so that we can give those young people who are still fasting a chance of success, so that they can stop their fast knowing full well that their cause has been just and that we as a Parliament of Canada have listened and will act in a very positive way.
